INDIA needs to strengthen oversight and intensify surveillance of the packaged water industry, the food regulator has said in a confidential directive to all states, days after announcing that a sample of the nation's biggest brand was found to be unsafe.

The directive, dated Nov 25 and reviewed by Reuters, comes amid consumer worries after the regulator said this week it found one sample of Bisleri, the country's biggest and best-known bottled water brand, was unsafe due to the presence of chemicals that health agencies say may cause cancer.
Bisleri has said its water is safe to consume and its testing found no problems.

The new government checks will increase regulatory oversight of PepsiCo, Tata Consumer, Coca-Cola and billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Consumer, who have all bet big on India's US$3.5 billion packaged water market.
The scrutiny will also cover the booming natural mineral water sector, which targets wealthy, health-conscious consumers.
These brands are more expensive than the standard US$0.20 variety of packaged water.

"Considering the importance of ensuring the safety and quality of packaged drinking water and mineral water, there is a need to strengthen regulatory oversight and intensify surveillance and enforcement activities to ensure strict compliance," said the regulator, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI).

The letter orders state officials to hold "regular inspections and risk-based sampling of packaged drinking water and mineral water", adding that "appropriate action shall be initiated in cases of non-compliance".
In Bisleri's case, the FSSAI has publicly said it will soon initiate prosecution proceedings against the company for non-compliance with food safety laws.
The FSSAI and state regulators have conducted many raids and pulled up companies for improper labelling, affecting restaurants such as Domino's and liquor companies including Diageo. — REUTERS
b11072f03d848ccd: MARSEILLE: Levski Sofia coach Julio Velazquez said violent fan clashes ahead of their Europa League game at Marseille on Thursday, which resulted in five supporters of the Bulgarian club being taken to hospital, were "unacceptable for football".
The lead-up to the match at the Stade Velodrome was marred by incidents in the stands between the two sets of supporters, including the throwing of projectiles and flares.
Several Marseille fans ran from the stand where they were situated about 10 minutes before kick-off, appearing to pursue a group of Bulgarian supporters.
They breached the stand designated for away fans, where around 500 Levski supporters were gathered.
"Five people were taken to hospital with eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder," the Marseille police prefecture told AFP.
"Six others were treated on site for various wounds."
The police source said all the people injured were Bulgarian and there was "no information at this stage regarding any arrests".
Security personnel eventually managed to restore calm as the game kicked off on time.
"It's a very regrettable episode - these are incidents which are unacceptable for football," said Velazquez.
"I support the fans who were caught up in this incident. I hope nothing serious has happened. I'm very saddened by this situation."
Ligue 1 club Marseille said it was "working to understand the precise circumstances of these incidents".
There were a few further flare-ups between the fans, notably during the half-time break.
"We are living through violent times in our society, so this is very, very regrettable," said Marseille coach Bruno Genesio.
The home team went on to win the game 1-0.

2d7c30d24cae2bdc: WEST PALM BEACH: As American families gathered to celebrate one of the biggest holidays of the year, US president Donald Trump on Thursday used the occasion of Thanksgiving to attack liberals, immigrants and a federal agency.
In a message on his Truth Social platform, Trump offered holiday greetings to people he accused of fraud, error or criminality.
"I would like to wish a very Happy Thanksgiving to all of those people that have worked so hard to bring our Country to the Radical Far Left," Trump said in the 461-word post.

The message was issued while the Republican president spent the family-oriented holiday at his Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach, Florida. He was expected to call US service members later on Thursday from his Mar-a-Lago estate.

In the holiday greeting, Trump accused his own government of falsifying US economic data. He warned of efforts by unnamed people to implement Muslim religious law and forcibly redistribute private property. He also described large numbers of US immigrants and people of Somali descent as jobless or criminal.

49a49942d09a5e0f: BOLOGNA: Rafael Jodar fought back from behind to send Spain past Austria and set up a Davis Cup semi-final meeting with Britain on Thursday.

Spain were leading the tie in Bologna 1-0 when Jodar lost his first set to Austrian Jurij Rodionov, but he then closed out the match and the quarter-final, losing only one game in the next two sets for a 2-6, 6-0, 6-1 triumph.
"It was very difficult for me because the first matches in tournaments are not easy," said the 20-year-old Jodar, who only made his Davis Cup debut in the qualifiers.

"I couldn't find my rhythm. In the second, the start of the second set, I started playing better and more aggressive and more solid from the baseline. I think that's what really helped me get into the match."
As Daniel Merida had earlier beaten Joel Schwaerzler 6-4, 6-4, there was no need for the doubles, meaning Carlos Alcaraz enjoyed a rest.
"It was amazing for me to give the first point for Spain. I think we have a good team here. I didn't play my best level today, but I got the win," Merida said.
Spain captain David Ferrer said Alcaraz, who has won three consecutive individual titles, including last week's ATP Finals, may be able to play in the singles against Britain on Saturday.
"I will see on Saturday. I don't know yet. But yeah, could be possible," said Ferrer of the seven-time Grand Slam champion.
Spain are bidding for a seventh Davis Cup title but their first since 2019, when Rafael Nadal played a starring role.
BRITAIN DOWN ZVEREV'S GERMANY
Britain booked their place in the semi-finals earlier in the day with a 2-1 victory over Alexander Zverev's Germany.
The world number one won his singles match, seeing off Arthur Fery, the man he beat in the Wimbledon semi-finals, 6-3, 6-2.
But that was only good enough to level the tie after Cameron Norrie had beaten Jan-Lennard Struff 6-3, 3-6, 6-2 in the opening singles.
The tie came down to the doubles, which pitted Britain's Henry Patten, the world number one in doubles, and Neal Skupski, ranked third, against the German pair of Kevin Krawietz and Tim Puetz.
The Britons sailed through the first set 6-2 but had to work harder in the second as it went all the way to a tie-break.
Skupski served for the match at 6-5 but a nervy volley went wide to give the Germans a lifeline. His next serve was clean and gave Britain their second match point.
This time, a brisk cross-court backhand sealed a 6-2, 7-6 (8/7) victory to send Britain into the semi-finals for the first time in seven years.
"It helps having a guy who can hit a return like that on match point," said Patten. "It makes it a lot easier for me."
"We regroup, we relax tomorrow and practise a little bit, and then get ready for whoever we play on Saturday," said Skupski.
Three-time reigning champions Italy will take on the Czech Republic in the first semi-final on Friday.

2625416c89a6479b: MADRID: Spanish authorities raced to contain potential damage to ecologically valuable Mediterranean waters on Thursday after a tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel capsized off Ibiza, leaving one person dead.

The Maltese-flagged Med Emre, a chemical products tanker travelling from the southern port of Algeciras to Barcelona, suffered the accident in the early hours of Thursday north of the popular holiday island, the Balearic Islands emergency services said.
The ship's 17 crew members were rescued, but one was later confirmed dead in hospital in Ibiza, while six suffered "minor injuries", notably hypothermia, the rescuers said.
According to maritime data tracking firm Kpler, the vessel was transporting around 66,000 barrels of refined products.
Spanish government sources said the ship was "lying keel up, which indicates that it is not currently sunk", revising an earlier statement that reported it had sunk.
Images shared by Spanish media showed the grey underbelly of a ship visible above the waves.
It was unclear what caused the accident.
A boat and a plane belonging to Spanish maritime rescue service Salvamento Maritimo had been sent to assess possible environmental damage, the Balearic emergency services added.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the government was "closely following" the situation.

Valencia maritime captain Elena Delgado said the small slick that had formed around the vessel "disappeared" at the end of the day and the ship had been secured by cable to a vessel from the Spanish maritime rescue service.
"The situation is stabilised," she said.
She added that experts would inspect the hull and submerged section on Friday morning before a decision was made on the planned salvage operation to tow the vessel.
VULNERABLE WATERS
Any pollution entering the water could affect tourism, fishing and Mediterranean seagrasses, which absorb substantial quantities of climate-heating carbon dioxide.
The area includes sites protected by the European Union's Natura 2000 network and is home to the critically endangered Balearic shearwater, said SEOBirdLife.
"Contact with the fuel may alter the impermeability and the thermal insulation of the birds' plumage, causing heat loss and hypothermia," the NGO warned.
Marine conservation group Oceana noted that the time of year was "key" for migratory species, including turtles, sharks, red tuna, pilot whales and striped dolphins.

But Emilio Rodriguez Diaz, a maritime security expert at the University of Cadiz, told Cadena SER radio that the incident was not comparable to the 2002 Prestige oil disaster, Spain's worst environmental accident.
That vessel broke into two, spilling more than 60,000 tonnes of fuel and blackening thousands of kilometres of Atlantic coastline, affecting Spain, Portugal and France.
The Med Emre was a modern ship, built in Turkiye in 2019, with a double hull that acted as "a kind of buffer that prevents the cargo... from being released into the environment", Diaz said.

ee92b61ed8b00824: TBILISI: Istanbul club Besiktas's supporters unfurled a pro-Palestinian banner during a Uefa Europa League match against Israeli side Hapoel Beer-Sheva in Georgia on Thursday, prompting a police response and sparking a diplomatic incident that led Turkey's foreign minister to contact his Georgian counterpart.
Turkish football fans clashed with police in Batumi, temporarily halting the match, which had been moved from Istanbul over security concerns.

Images from the stadium showed Besiktas supporters displaying a banner reading "Revolt against the occupation, freedom for Palestine", waving Palestinian flags and chanting anti-Israel slogans before police intervened.
Police used pepper spray against fans, some of whom required medical attention, Turkey's private DHA news agency reported.
The match was suspended in the 26th minute because of disturbances in the stands, with Danish referee Morten Krogh sending both teams to the dressing rooms.
Turkey's football federation strongly condemned what it described as the "unacceptable" conduct of Georgian police towards Besiktas supporters.

"We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, behaviour and actions directed at Besiktas supporters inside and outside the stadium before and during the Uefa Europa League match," the federation said in a statement.
'Disproportionate use of force'

Uefa announced last month that the fixture would be moved to Georgia after Turkish authorities informed European football's governing body that, "for safety and security reasons", the match could not be hosted in Istanbul.
Besiktas said they had lodged a complaint with Uefa over what they described as the "disproportionate" use of force by Georgian police.
"We have launched initiatives with our consulate general in Batumi and Uefa regarding the disproportionate use of force against our supporters by security forces," the club said.
Besiktas added that they would closely monitor the situation until all of their supporters had returned safely to Turkey.
After the match, which finished 2-1 to Besiktas, Hapoel Beer-Sheva posted a message on social media directed to their travelling supporters.

"Please act responsibly, show restraint and use your best judgement as you leave the stadium and make your way to your accommodation. Follow the instructions of the Georgian security forces, who are responsible for ensuring your safety," the club posted in Hebrew on X.
Turkey's president Recep Tayyip Erdogan spoke by phone with Besiktas chairman Serdal Adali and said he was closely following developments, the club said.
Several people were believed to have been detained after clashes erupted in the stands at the stadium in the Black Sea city of Batumi, local media reported.
Besiktas supporters scuffled with police and hurled objects at officers as they attempted to make arrests, according to live television footage.
The incidents prompted Turkish foreign minister Hakan Fidan to call his Georgian counterpart, Maka Botchorishvili.
"Officials from the Turkish embassy in Tbilisi and the consulate general in Batumi are at the stadium," a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
"All necessary steps are being taken to ensure the safety of our citizens and protect their rights."
Relations between Turkey and Israel have deteriorated sharply since the outbreak of the Gaza war.
Erdogan, a staunch supporter of the Palestinian cause and a frequent critic of Israel, has repeatedly accused Israel of committing "genocide" in Gaza.
Pro-Palestinian banners and chants are seen or heard frequently at Turkish football matches, particularly since the start of the war.

PRODUCER Datin Dr Wendy Wong took up scuba diving to better understand the challenges faced by her cast and crew while filming 'Takdir Terakhir: Last Dive'.
The 28-year entertainment industry veteran attended the course alongside co-producer Datuk Nancie Foo, with both women diving to a depth of 7m.

"Actually, the course requires at least five days, but I could only attend for three days due to time constraints," Wong said at the recent launch of the film's poster, trailer and soundtrack singing competition.
"I thought they would take me down just 3m, but we ended up reaching 7m. I was terrified, but the experience gave me huge respect for those who work underwater."

The experience gave her a better understanding of the strict safety protocols and time limits involved in underwater filming, as well as the additional challenges posed by unpredictable weather and murky waters.
"Previously, when the crew surfaced and needed an hour to rest, I might have wondered why they could not dive straight back in.
"But after taking the course, I began to understand. I would also become anxious whenever they spent a long time underwater, knowing their air supply was limited."
Working with five divers with disabilities also required changes to the production's logistics, including arrangements for accessible accommodation and toilet facilities.
"There were many details to consider. Some hotels had been booked, but we had to change them because their facilities were unsuitable.
"We learnt a great deal during filming. If we made any mistakes, we apologise and will strive to do better," Wong added.
The film also features special appearances by Datuk Dr Ras Adiba Radzi and Fauziah Latiff, and stars Shiqin Kamal, Aniq Durar, Fify Azmi, Amerul Affendi and Sandra Lim.
Ras Adiba said: "Hopefully, this film will open a new chapter for persons with disabilities, encouraging more productions to give them opportunities to act."
'Takdir Terakhir: Last Dive' hits cinemas on Dec 3.
de9e45996772580b: MEXICO CITY: Mexico's central bank raised its 2026 economic growth forecast to 1.9% on Thursday after stronger-than-expected activity in the third quarter, even as it warned that investment is likely to remain subdued because of uncertainty over trade ties with the US.
Banxico, as the Bank of Mexico is known, lifted its forecast for 2026 GDP growth from 1.5% previously in its quarterly report.

"The revision primarily reflects economic activity in the third quarter that performed better than anticipated," the central bank said, adding that it expects growth to moderate in the fourth quarter before gradually picking up again.
Banxico said domestic investment would likely remain "relatively weak," citing uncertainty tied to Mexico's trade relationship with the US and the review of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement.

Mexico's economy is tightly linked to that of the US, its largest trading partner. President Claudia Sheinbaum said last week she had a "very good meeting" with US president Donald Trump as the two governments continue talks aimed at easing trade tensions.

Banxico also flagged a widening split inside Mexico's manufacturing sector. It said strong US demand for goods linked to artificial intelligence has fueled Mexican electronics exports, but that this has translated only weakly into broader manufacturing growth because the sector depends heavily on imported inputs.

Data released earlier this week by statistics agency INEGI showed Mexico's economy grew 0.9% in the July-September quarter from the previous quarter on a seasonally adjusted basis, after a sharp rebound in the second quarter. GDP expanded 3.3% from a year earlier.

On inflation, Banxico raised its fourth-quarter 2026 forecast for both headline and core inflation to 3.7% from 3.5% previously. Still, it kept its longer-term outlook unchanged and continued to project that both measures will converge to its 3% inflation target in 2027.
The central bank added that in 2028, it expects the economy to accelerate, forecasting GDP growth of 2.5%.

VALENCIA: Francesco Bagnaia's Ducati career will end on the sidelines after the team said on Wednesday that the twice MotoGP champion was unfit for this weekend's season finale in Valencia.
Bagnaia suffered a painful crash on lap one in Qatar this month when Fermin Aldeguer collided with his Ducati's rear tyre, resulting in a fractured foot and the sprint being red-flagged.
The 29-year-old missed the Portuguese Grand Prix, where team mate Marc Marquez won his eighth MotoGP title.
"A return to the track slips away for Pecco: the final medical checks carried out this morning before the start did not give the green light to get back on the bike," Ducati said in a statement.

"Taking his place, just as in Portugal, will be Iker Lecuona, who is competing on home turf in Valencia and arrives energised and positive after scoring points in both races of the Portuguese weekend."

Bagnaia won MotoGP championships in 2022 and 2023 before finishing runner-up in 2024. But his fortunes have dipped since Marc Marquez's arrival in 2025, with the Spaniard winning the championship in each of the last two seasons.

"Still, it remains a special weekend: the farewell weekend to the Rossa of Borgo Panigale, closing a wonderful, success-filled story made of a love and a passion destined to last forever, with the winningest rider in Ducati's MotoGP history, boasting 31 wins to his name," Ducati added.

Bagnaia will join Aprilia in 2027 after signing a four-year deal with the Italian manufacturer, with KTM rider Pedro Acosta set to replace him at the factory Ducati team and partner Marquez in an all-Spanish lineup. — REUTERS
77a3578b7baf674f: OSLO: The head of the Norwegian Football Federation Lise Klaveness, a fierce critic of Fifa president Gianni Infantino, acknowledged Thursday it would be "difficult" to topple him but the possibility was "still in play".

Klaveness has been critical of Infantino since 2022 when the World Cup was held in Qatar, and called for his resignation in August after several controversies during this year's World Cup hosted by the United States, Canada and Mexico.
"It will be difficult" to dethrone Infantino, Klaveness, a lawyer and former national squad player, told foreign media in Oslo on Thursday.

While European football confederation Uefa has rallied around French football chief Philippe Diallo's candidacy to take over the Fifa presidency in a March election, Infantino, who is running for re-election, still enjoys the support of the African, South American and Asian confederations, and is seen as the favourite.
"You cannot really know what's going to happen in such a volatile political world," Klaveness, 45, argued.
"So it might end up with a different candidate than Infantino for very many reasons."
"But as it seems now, he has a lot of support."

While the African (CAF) and South American (Conmebol) football confederations have reaffirmed their backing for Infantino, Klaveness pointed out that it is not they who vote, but the national federations, and that each vote is secret.
"That's why it's still in play," she said.
She also said she hoped that Diallo and the third candidate, Kozo Tashima, honorary president of the Japanese federation, would manage to join forces against Infantino.

At the head of Fifa since 2016, Infantino has been involved in several recent controversies, including accusations of running a one-man show, awarding a Fifa "peace prize" to Donald Trump, lifting the suspension of USA forward Folarin Balogun during the 2026 World Cup, and floating plans - later abandoned - to sell stakes in World Cup commercial rights.
04e98d86c0f30aed: MOSCOW: Kazakhstan's president Kassym-Jomart Tokayev advanced his country's AI ambitions at Russia's main AI conference on Thursday, telling President Vladimir Putin that Russian companies Sberbank and Yandex were welcome in Kazakhstan's market.

Tokayev's visit to Moscow comes a month after he held a meeting with Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang in the Kazakh capital Astana, during which Freedom Holding, a big Kazakhstan bank, said it was placing a large order for Nvidia's B300 chips.

Russia's supercomputers are built on older versions of Nvidia chips. It is struggling to develop its AI industry and catch up with leaders US and China, as US sanctions over its war in Ukraine have halted its imports of the US-made chips needed to train AI models.

Many Russian companies operate in Central Asian nations without restrictions, taking advantage of these countries' continued relations with the West, as well as their proximity and business ties to China. Closer Russia-Kazakhstan cooperation on AI and a growing Russian corporate footprint in the ex-Soviet state could boost this trend.
"We are pleased to see Russian companies' progress in our market, and they can rely on our comprehensive assistance," Tokayev told Putin ahead of Sberbank's AI Journey conference in Moscow.

Tokayev said that Russia-based technology group Yandex was the biggest employer in Kazakhstan, and a large delegation of his country's AI entrepreneurs and officials responsible for AI joined the president on his visit to Moscow.

Sberbank unveiled new versions of its GigaChat AI model and its video-generating Kandinsky model on Thursday, and presented Tokayev and Putin with a new generation of its Grin AI-powered humanoid robots.
Russia does not produce its own advanced chips, and its supercomputers used to train AI models were built before the war in Ukraine began and the West imposed sanctions.

"A shortage of electricity, power grids, and complex component base are becoming bottlenecks in the technological race. Overcoming these barriers requires new, massive investments," Putin told the conference.

A new Russian decree allows Russian companies to use data centres located abroad with the permission of security services. Putin signed it after Ukrainian drones targeted Russian data centres and supercomputers earlier this year.

Sberbank and Yandex did not publicly say whether they would respond by moving some of their services to data centres in other countries, as information about data centres at Russian companies is confidential.

Sberbank chief executive German Gref visited China in May to discuss access to the most advanced China-made chips, but a person with knowledge of those discussions told Reuters the talks were inconclusive.

The Russian daily Kommersant reported on Thursday, citing sources, that Gref, who was born in Soviet Kazakhstan, was also in regular discussions about AI development with Tokayev and was a frequent visitor to the Kazakh capital.
Sberbank did not comment on the report.

During Huang's October visit to Kazakhstan, Freedom Holding, led by Russian-born entrepreneur Timur Turlov -- who renounced his Russian citizenship in 2022 and also severed business links to Russia -- announced plans to build a US$2 billion Sovereign AI Hub in Kazakhstan.

"We are already placing an order for our first computing cluster powered by Nvidia's latest B300 chips, with up to 300 servers and a total investment of hundreds of millions of dollars," Turlov said at the time.

Huang, who this month resigned and was then reinstated to his role as CEO, also confirmed during the October visit that Nvidia had invested in Kazakhstan's AI video generation startup Higgsfield as part of the statup's US$400-million funding round.
9432a4fdcf7e6802: HONG KONG: Hundreds of people paid their respects Thursday at the site of a horrific fire that ripped through a Hong Kong apartment complex and killed 168 people one year ago, as authorities in the Chinese territory kept a wary eye.

The world's deadliest residential building blaze since 1980 began on the afternoon of Nov 26, 2025 and raged for two days, gutting seven of Wang Fuk Court's eight high-rise buildings that were home to some 4,600 people.
Authorities in the Chinese territory -- where Beijing has tightened its grip in recent years -- appeared worried about commemorations taking on a political tone and held no official memorial.

Police on Thursday kept a low profile as mourners, some weeping and hugging, laid bouquets at a small park in the shadow of the ruined buildings, as well as notes, toys, bottles of water and even pet food.
As dusk fell, officials began moving some of the hundreds of bouquets, citing the need to create space, mourners said.
This angered some of the people who had come to pay their respects, and several began moving the flowers themselves.
"This bouquet is a token of my love for my mother," said Polly, who lost her parent in the tragedy.
"It seems even the gift I gave my mother is being taken away from me."
The government said in a statement that flowers and other offerings would be moved to places of worship.
Ip, whose father and aunt perished, folded 168 paper cranes -- a symbol of mourning -- to hang them around the area with his wife and son.
"Those who passed away were gone. Perhaps it is better to make these (paper cranes) as if they will fly away," his wife said.
"It eases my heart, knowing they are no longer trapped in such a dark place."
'Grief and outrage'
The blaze was Hong Kong's worst disaster in more than seven decades, and a shock to the 7.5 million residents of one of Asia's safest cities.
The city's number two official Eric Chan had said the government would offer help to "lawful" memorial events, but warned against "acts of disorder".
The Chinese government's Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office spoke this week against attempts to "cause chaos" under the guise of commemorations.
Human Rights Watch said the Hong Kong government was "using Beijing's tactics of shutting out the voices of the victims and promising an elusive accountability".

John Burns, a politics professor at the University of Hong Kong, told AFP that the space for public anger and criticism is "much narrower" than before Beijing imposed a national security law in 2020, following huge and sometimes violent pro-democracy protests.
A government spokesman said officials allowed some former residents on Thursday to visit the housing estate, which has been cordoned off for nearly a year.
Some Catholic and Buddhist places of worship also hosted events this week to pray for the dead.
'Perfect storm'
Last month, city leader John Lee led some of his ministers in bowing in apology, and the housing chief resigned.
A report from a judge-led inquiry said the fire was likely started by a cigarette and spread quickly via netting on building facades.
Authorities said in an inquiry report the tragedy was a "perfect storm" exposing longstanding flaws in regulation and a slack enforcement attitude.
Police told AFP that 40 people have been arrested in connection with the blaze.
Eric Lai, a senior fellow at Georgetown Center for Asian Law, said that the government wanted to "tame public grievance" over its response.
"But at the same time they remain anxious of silencing dissenting voices," he told AFP.
Former resident Dorz Cheung told AFP that he still felt "very, very, very angry" about the government's response to oversights exposed in the tragedy.
"There are still so many emotions... anger, deep sadness, they're all around."
7fe4796c7e05c4dd: DOHA: George Russell on Thursday responded to Max Verstappen's taunting putdowns of his talent and potential, congratulating him on his Las Vegas win and conceding that that he was amused by the Dutchman's comments, but not cowed.

The Mercedes driver, who finished ninth behind Red Bull's Verstappen after hitting the barriers in the closing laps of last Sunday's Las Vegas Grand Prix, told reporters that he was putting their latest feud behind him.
"I don't really have much to say, to be honest," he said during a press conference ahead of this weekend's Qatar Grand Prix, the penultimate race of the season.
"I found some of his comments post-race quite amusing, but at the end of the day, he drove an incredible race, won it and can afford to say what he wants. So, from my side, I am moving on."
Four-time world champion Verstappen had been acerbic in his comments, reopening old wounds in a two-year-old rivalry that has seen the duo engaging in vitriolic exchanges and trading insults.

Last weekend, Russell tangled with Verstappen in final practice and declared that his actions on track were like "screwing a person over" and added that he did this "week in and week out, with everybody accepting it".
"I'm not going to accept somebody screwing me over like this and then walking around like they are bigger and better than everyone else. Someone has to stand up to that guy," said the Briton.
After the race, Verstappen said he was not bothered at all by Russell, dismissing him as a driver who is "so far below my level".
He added, in relation to Russell's crash, which dropped him to ninth after previously battling for the lead, that "karma is a bitch!"
"It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror and I saw what was happening. I was like 'Fantastic! My day is only getting better' and when I crossed the line in first, my day was complete."
Asked on Thursday if he had any answer to those comments, Russell said: "No. Not really. I guess I stand by what I said after practice, but he was the one who went out and won... I didn't.
"I'm sure he had a bit of a laugh about it - and it was reasonably amusing – so from my side, it's a new weekend, a new race, and I will try to focus on the driving and move on."
'Do talking on track'
Outgoing world champion Lando Norris, who is a friend of both drivers, said it was time for Russell to prove himself on the track.
"This is a sport where you want to prove that you're better than everyone else," he said.
"So you can either do your talking on the track or in front of a camera. It normally helps when you back it up on track.

"That's what everyone, at the end of the day, really cares about, but I still respect both drivers a lot. Obviously, Max has proved to everyone what he's capable of - and George is still, I think, yet to prove what he's capable of."

b2a86b0e41cd1284: KUWAIT CITY: A drone attack in Kuwait killed two Italian technicians working on an air defence system on Thursday, marking the first fatal strike in the Gulf state for months.

Both Italy and Kuwait confirmed the deaths, blaming the attack on Iran. But Tehran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi insisted in calls to his Kuwaiti and Italian counterparts that it was not behind the deadly strike.
Iran has in the last week ratcheted up attacks on Kuwait and Gulf neighbour Bahrain while it continues to fight the US for control of the contested Strait of Hormuz.

"Around 2pm today, several Iranian-made drones targeted Kuwaiti military installations, including an air-defence detection station where two Italian technicians from Rheinmetall were working," Italian foreign minister Antonio Tajani told the Senate.
Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni took to social media to offer her condolences.
"My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families," she wrote on X.
But Iran was quick to refute the allegations that it was behind the deadly attack.

Araghchi held phone calls with both his Kuwaiti counterpart Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah and Italian counterpart Antonio Tajani to deny Tehran's involvement, according to Iran's state TV and foreign ministry.
In his call with Tajani, "Araghchi stated that Iran had no role or involvement whatsoever in the occurrence of this event," the Iranian foreign ministry said in a statement.
Iran's top diplomat added that Tehran was prepared to cooperate with Kuwait and Italy to "determine the origin of the incident", the ministry said.
He also offered a joint probe in his call with Al-Sabah, state TV reported.
Armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi had earlier refuted the claims that Iran was involved and blamed false flag operations by Israel and the US for the attack, without providing evidence.
"No military or offensive operations have been conducted by the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the region," he said, state TV reported.
But EU chief Ursula von der Leyen called for more pressure on Tehran after the deaths.
"We must step up pressure on Iran to put an end to these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf," she wrote on social media.
The Kuwaiti defence ministry had earlier said that at least four people were injured in the incident, saying several drones had targeted an unspecified, vital location in the country.
Air defences
The attack comes days after Kuwait activated its air defences last week to counter drone strikes launched by Iran -- the first since early September.

The conflict -- which began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February -- has seen the Gulf states caught in the crossfire, with US military facilities and energy installations on their soil targeted.
The US and Iran are in a standoff over the vital Strait of Hormuz, with the US military working to escort ships transiting the waterway in defiance of Tehran's attempts to close the waterway.
Further south, the war between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis continued to rage, following a week that saw the two sides trade heavy blows.

The Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said the Iran-backed group struck a refinery in southern Saudi Arabia's Jazan, which state media said killed one person and triggered a temporary shutdown of some operations.
It marked the latest in a series of barrages targeting major energy installations in the kingdom.
The coalition also claimed to have destroyed a ballistic missile launcher in Houthi territory that was used in the attack on the refinery.
The exchanges between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen have become near-daily in the country's revived civil war, which first began more than a decade ago.
Later Thursday, Houthi media citing their health ministry published figures saying 19 civilians had been killed in the past 48 hours by "Saudi-led aggression".

Earlier, the coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognised government, said its forces had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital of Riyadh overnight, where residents and an AFP journalist heard an explosion.
6f743fb2de6bee4e: DOHA: Charles Leclerc on Thursday insisted that he does not have number one status at Ferrari, as the team regrouped following last weekend's shambolic show in Las Vegas, ahead of the Qatar Grand Prix.

1a2186348403f363: WEST PALM BEACH: US president Donald Trump said Thursday he had asked Vladimir Putin to "pull back all military aggression" against Europe, in a fresh shift in tone towards the Russian leader he called his friend just last week.
Trump said he had made the request to Putin when they met in China last week, adding that he thought it would help lead to a deal to end Moscow's grinding war in Ukraine.
Trump's comments come a day after he hosted Nato chief Mark Rutte in Florida, after which the two leaders issued a joint statement calling on Russia not to expand the Ukraine war.

"During my conversations in China with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe," Trump said on his Truth Social network.
Trump said he had done so "in the hopes that a Deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine, and made quickly."
"I really believe this is a strong possibility -- Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, A COMPLETE BLOODBATH -- and will be a Great Tribute to everyone!"

The statement did not specify which territories Trump meant -- and did not specifically include Ukraine, which Russia invaded in February 2022, kicking off the largest war in Europe since World War II.
But European nations have been increasingly concerned by what they regard as Russian provocations, including three Russian cruise missiles landing in Poland last week.
In their joint statement on Wednesday, Trump and Nato's Rutte said they "discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war."
Trump, who is spending the US Thanksgiving holiday at his Mar-a-Lago resort, reposted the joint statement with Rutte on Truth Social shortly before his new comments on Putin.
In a notable contrast with Trump's recent criticisms of Ukraine for striking targets deep inside Russia, the US leader made no call for Kyiv to show similar restraint.
'Deadlock'
Trump's tone appeared markedly different to when Trump met Putin in the Chinese city of Shenzhen last week, both face-to-face and together with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
On that occasion, a smiling Trump welcomed Putin by saying "Who is he? He's my friend," before warmly shaking hands with the Russian leader.
The "friend" comment in particular renewed concerns in Kyiv and European capitals that Trump was once again pivoting towards the Russian leader he has long been close to.

Trump has often appeared more willing to blame Ukraine for Russia's invasion, and has had tense relations with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky since their televised blow-up in the Oval Office in February 2025.
The US envoys on the Ukraine war, Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and business friend Steve Witkoff, have been accused of a similar willingness to take Moscow's side.
In an interview with the German MD Meets Podcast on Wednesday, Kushner said that Putin had "showed restraint" because he had "agreed not to use nuclear weapons."

Kushner also described the Russian leader, whom he has met several times, as a "grandmaster of politics" -- while calling the Ukraine conflict "a proxy war where Europe is funding and arming Ukraine against Russia."
But he acknowledged that the issue of territory in eastern Ukraine claimed by Moscow remained a sticking point with Putin.

"What Steve and I have deciphered from having many, many hours with President Putin and from the Russian team, is that you know the territorial issue is right now a little bit of a deadlock," he said.
And he warned against any downward spiral in the Ukraine war, saying it "it won't take a lot of miscalculation for this thing to escalate massively."

3b2b7b1913cdbfc6: Chinese and North Korean state-sponsored hacking crews are among the growing number of groups known for using the ARTEX pentesting tool in attacks, Microsoft said this week.
ARTEX is an open source, AI-powered penetration testing framework that attackers have adopted to automate reconnaissance, credential attacks, and exploitation since its public release in July.

Campaigns that have been linked to ARTEX have targeted cloud environments, IT software like ConnectWise, and financial institutions globally, sometimes reaching privileged access in under three hours.

Salt Typhoon is arguably the most recognizable name on the list of ARTEX beneficiaries – the group responsible for attacks on telcos AT&T and Verizon, US government systems, UK prime minister's aides, and more.
The lesser-known Crystal Typhoon – the group behind the ArcaneDoor attacks back when Microsoft called it Storm-1849 – was also named alongside it, as were North Korea's Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet.
Microsoft also named China-state-aligned Storm-0940, linked to the ConnectWise compromise, and financially motivated, Cambodia-based Storm-3358. It had previously reported both groups' use of ARTEX.
Chinese cybersecurity company ThreatBook claimed ownership of ARTEX in November. GitHub user "Autumn-27" originally published its source code with a Chinese-language interface in July.
Various forks of the repo, which was taken down in October, have meant that the same framework is available in multiple languages.
According to Infrawatch, there are more than 130 variants of ARTEX in circulation, and it is the most widely used agentic offensive framework (AOF) at present.

Like other offensive security tools adopted by criminals, ARTEX can lower the effort required to mount attacks. Experienced groups can also use it to automate repetitive work and pursue multiple avenues at once.

As Microsoft echoed this week, after the FBI and AWS issued their warnings earlier this month, ARTEX is proving to be a useful tool for the more sophisticated groups to streamline and hasten their attacks too.
It's being used to help attackers steal AI and cloud credentials at "industrial scale," as AWS put it, which provide attackers access to advanced models for free.
Microsoft says ARTEX can progress from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access within minutes, depending on its configuration and the target's defenses.

"In the past few weeks, we've reported several distinct campaigns that abused ARTEX to search public repositories for exposed secrets, enable supply chain compromise, and scan internet-facing systems for exploitation," its threat intelligence team blogged. "These campaigns illustrate how threat actors use ARTEX to automate various stages of the attack chain.

"Threat actors define scope and targets for ARTEX, which then uses AI agents to set verifiable goals, define tactical steps for each stage of the operation, use tools to attack targets, create graphs to track discovered systems and results of actions, and report back to the threat actor."

Notably, ARTEX does not offer any new attack techniques. All of the tool's capabilities were previously known to the cybersecurity world, but its value lies in the automation capabilities it offers users, chaining attacks at machine speed.

In the UK NCSC's warning about AOFs this week, it said the key strengths of this technology are its speed, its thoroughness in probing target systems for weaknesses, how it learns from failures instantly, and that it is inexpensive to run at scale.
AOFs' speed comes at a cost, however. These tools are noisy, the NCSC said, making them easier to detect in network logs and by defensive solutions.

f97ba7ee0bd5f5eb: The independent Ladybird web browser has reached an important milestone: an alpha test version. What's more, it works well. These may not be the criteria by which some will judge it, though.

Earlier this week, the developer behind the Ladybird web browser announced that Ladybird is now in alpha. We've given it a brief test, and it performed very well. It's more stable and works better than its alpha label would suggest.
There are downloads available, covering macOS on Apple Silicon, as well as for Linux on x86-64; for the latter, there's a Flatpak package, as well as native Ubuntu and Fedora packages.

It's an open source project, so you can download the source code from the GitHub repository and compile it yourself, but in an unusual move, back in June the project announced that the developers would no longer accept public code contributions.

We first mentioned Ladybird as part of our early 2022 look at its original parent project – SerenityOS: Remarkable project with its own JS-capable web browser. Both the name and the date are significant: the former is a nod to the Serenity prayer, recited at the end of Alcoholics Anonymous meetings. The date of the article is because it's well before the launch of ChatGPT at the end of 2022.

About a year and a half later, we reported that Serenity OS turns five and emits first offspring, Ladybird. Both the OS and the browser were still hand-coded, but now the browser could be compiled and run on other OSes. That freed it up to call upon external libraries which didn't exist for SerenityOS.

Earlier this year, we wrote Ladybird flutters toward Rust with a little help from AI. At one point, developer Andreas Kling used Apple's Swift language, but this year, he changed course and adopted Rust instead, using LLM tools to convert some existing code. Some will dismiss Ladybird because of this, but as our first coverage shows, the browser and its original host OS were established projects before the current wave of AI-assisted development.

Kling does use LLMs, but Ladybird is not some sloppy vibe-coded effort. The macOS download is 68.4 MB in size, which in 2026 is remarkably small. The Flatpak is larger – about 111 MB – but it also pulls in some KDE dependencies which increase its size.

We tested it on Pop!_OS. It handles sites such as The Register and Hacker News and everything else we tried perfectly, and took just 6 percent of our Dell XPS13's CPU to play full-screen HD video from YouTube smoothly. In our short testing, we saw no crashes, hesitation, or any other problems at all.
The developers nevertheless warn that the alpha can crash, some websites will not work, and they make no security guarantees at this stage.

The use of LLMs will put some people off. However, this is not the only controversial thing about the project. As we have noted in our previous coverage, Ladybird belongs to the same political wing of the FOSS movement as Omarchy, XLibre, and other right-wing projects. If the LLM use doesn't put you off, the political views may. On the other hand, as we've seen from our earlier coverage of Omarchy and XLibre, the same factors also attract others.

The modern Web is an entire complex compute platform in its own right, and currently, only three tools support it – and two of those are interrelated. The dominant engines are Google's Blink, used by Chrome and other Chromium browsers; Apple's WebKit, used by Safari; and Mozilla's Gecko, used by Firefox. Blink was forked from WebKit.

Some day, when the Servo project matures some more, it may be another. Even so, today, the first preliminary release of Ladybird means that there are now four competitive modern browser engines. That's a significant step. ®

c6c514a3477bed88: FEW healthcare ideas have the potential to deliver such immediate benefits to underserved communities as the Health Ministry's proposed cottage hospital initiative.

At first glance, the concept appears straightforward. Selected rural health clinics will be upgraded with observation wards and enhanced medical capabilities, allowing patients to receive a broader range of treatments closer to home.
Yet behind this modest proposal lies a potentially transformative shift in how healthcare is delivered to some of Malaysia's most geographically isolated communities.

In his winding-up speech during the debate on the Supply Bill 2027 in the Dewan Rakyat recently, Health Minister Datuk Seri Dr Dzulkefly Ahmad said the Health Ministry has identified four existing health clinics under the concept: Sungai Asap in Sarawak; Telupid and Nabawan in Sabah; and Tekek on Pulau Tioman, Pahang.
Their selection is no accident. Sungai Asap is about 184km from Bintulu, while Telupid sits some 125km from Sandakan.
Nabawan, meanwhile, serves communities deep in Sabah's interior, far from Keningau, the nearest urban centre with more comprehensive medical facilities.
Together, they exemplify the geographical challenges that many rural Malaysians face in accessing healthcare.
The objective is clear: improve access to inpatient care, reduce the need for long-distance travel and ease congestion at larger hospitals.
These facilities are intended to serve as a bridge between ordinary health clinics and major referral hospitals, bringing healthcare closer to the people who need it most.
While each location has its own unique characteristics, they share a common challenge. Distance.

Nowhere is this challenge more evident than in Sarawak, whose immense land area, dispersed population and vast network of rural settlements mean that healthcare accessibility remains a constant concern.
Sungai Asap was established in the late 1990s as the resettlement area for communities displaced by the Bakun Dam, including many Orang Ulu families from the Sungai Balui basin.
Today, despite the area's development, residents of Sungai Asap and other interior settlements still face long journeys to major hospitals.
Such trips can be physically demanding, time-consuming and costly, particularly for the elderly, patients requiring regular monitoring and lower-income families.
The situation is equally relevant in Sabah.
Communities served by clinics in Telupid and Nabawan frequently live significant distances from specialist medical facilities.
Rural residents sometimes have little choice but to spend hours on the road to obtain treatment that could potentially be delivered closer to home if enhanced facilities were available locally.
For patients and caregivers alike, reducing travel time can greatly improve quality of life.
Pulau Tioman presents another compelling case. Islanders contend with geographical constraints that mainland residents rarely experience.
Accessing advanced medical care often means travelling by sea and then continuing onward to larger healthcare centres.
Weather conditions and transportation arrangements can further complicate matters.
Viewed collectively, these locations illustrate why the initiative deserves serious consideration. The Health Ministry is not simply upgrading buildings.
It is reimagining healthcare delivery in places where geography remains one of the greatest barriers to timely treatment.
The proposal is also notable because it emphasises the intelligent use of existing infrastructure.
Rather than embarking solely on costly new hospital construction projects, the government is exploring ways to strengthen facilities that are already embedded within communities.
This approach could shorten implementation timelines while delivering meaningful improvements in patient care.
Equally important is the potential impact on overcrowded hospitals.
Patients requiring observation, follow-up treatment or less complex inpatient care may no longer need to travel to major hospitals unnecessarily.
This would allow larger institutions to focus on highly specialised procedures and critical cases.
Success here will ultimately depend on execution. Adequate staffing, appropriate equipment, continuous training and sustainable funding will remain essential.
Rural communities deserve not only buildings, but also quality services delivered consistently and professionally.
Nonetheless, the underlying principle is both practical and compassionate. Communities should not face unnecessary disadvantages simply because of where they live.

If successful, the cottage hospital initiative under the Madani Reform Agenda championed by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim could emerge as one of the country's most meaningful healthcare reforms.
It reflects a simple but powerful belief: quality healthcare should reach the people, wherever they may live.
* The writer is a former Bernama chief executive officer and editor-in-chief

9c0e60c0432004ce: THE unexpected corruption investigation into Shanghai party chief Chen Jining, once seen as a strong contender for China's highest leadership body, challenges assumptions long used by diplomats and analysts to anticipate Beijing's opaque power moves.

Experts said the Shanghai party secretary post, a position once held by both President Xi Jinping and former president Jiang Zemin, was a well-trodden route to the party's top leadership posts that now appeared much less predictable.

"There is no more straight-forward pathway from Shanghai party secretary to the Politburo Standing Committee," said Wen-Ti Sung, a nonresident fellow at the Atlantic Council's Global China Hub, adding that political loyalty was the main criterion.

The sudden announcement of the investigation into Chen, an Imperial College London graduate in environmental engineering who stood out among his peers for having spent roughly a decade in Britain, surprised both the diplomatic and business communities.
Over nearly four decades, eight former Shanghai party chiefs were promoted to the Politburo Standing Committee. Chen's predecessor Li Qiang is now premier and sits on the current committee.
Chen, 62, was seen as a strong contender for elevation to the committee in the party's leadership reshuffle during the 21st Party Congress next year.
Xi is "clearing the ground" before the congress, sweeping aside entrenched political customs and older networks to build a more ideologically aligned leadership lineup, a senior Asian diplomat said.
China's anti-graft watchdog announced on Tuesday that Chen was under investigation for "suspected serious violations of discipline and law", a euphemism commonly used for corruption in China.
He had an unusual rise through China's official ranks. An environmental scientist by training, he rose through ​China's elite Tsinghua University, Xi's alma mater, to become its president.

He entered the government as China's environmental protection minister in 2015 — just as Xi made the area a priority — before becoming mayor of Beijing. He joined the Politburo in 2022 and was named party boss of Shanghai, China's financial hub.

A champion for artificial intelligence development in Shanghai and Beijing, Chen was last seen in public last week holding separate meetings with Chinese shipping company COSCO and the chairman of Swiss pharmaceutical firm Roche.

The brief turnaround between Chen's last public appearance and the probe is unusual. Senior party officials usually disappear from public view for extended stretches before an investigation is officially announced.
Xi's dismantling of reform-era term limit norms and promotion of loyalists, together with the high-pressure anti-graft drive, have disrupted established routes to elevation and succession.
In 2017, Sun Zhengcai, a former Chongqing party chief and Politburo member, who was viewed as a potential future leader, was abruptly removed and later sentenced to life in prison for corruption.

Chen is the fourth Politburo member investigated in just over a year as Xi's anti-corruption purge reaches the party's innermost circle, having already ensnared Central Military Commission vice-chairmen Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, as well as former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui.
"Chen's purge is particularly shocking in that he poses no military threat, and doesn't deviate from Xi on major symbolic issues like ethnic policy," Sung said.
"But he got purged anyway, so far without even an explanation. The shock is bound to reverberate."

eefc75c7c3c24ae0: Years of technical debt, increasingly complex systems, and underinvestment in IT operations have left organizations vulnerable to major outages, according to Forrester.
The analyst pointed to a seven-day stretch in November when failures disrupted Microsoft 365, US air traffic control, banking, and other critical services.
The coinciding outages provoked "a slew of conspiracy theories about cyberattacks and AI," Forrester said.

"The real culprit is tragically mundane: the culmination of decades of technical debt, the frenetic buildout of massively complex and highly interdependent systems, the concentration of risk, and the underinvestment in advanced operations."

Forrester urged technology suppliers and in-house IT teams to prioritize resilience as their systems grow more complex. Otherwise, "the tech estate will collapse like a house of cards, taking down consumer and business trust with it."

Earlier this month, Microsoft was left struggling to restore many of its cloud services after a core process running on some servers became "overwhelmed" and its attempts to fix the problem failed. Some of its services did not recover for another 24 hours.

In October, Google Cloud blamed a "power event" for taking down multiple online products for customers in Western Europe. Affected services included BigQuery Data Transfer Service, Cloud Filestore, Cloud Run, Google App Engine, and Google Kubernetes Engine.
In October last year, a major outage impacted Amazon Web Services (AWS), with even Amazon's own web page reported to be offline and dozens of other online services and websites affected.

Aviation and banking were also hit this month. A communications outage triggered a nationwide ground stop in the US on November 13, while incidents involving JPMorgan Chase, United Airlines, Apple, Workday, Gmail, and other services added to the sense of widespread instability.
"Claims that these were all part of one connected cyberattack or conspiracy are highly unlikely. The real story is much more mundane," the report said.
Forrester argued that organizations have prioritized visible improvements over repairs to the underlying technology.

"Modernization investments have favored visible change over structural renewal," wrote report authors Lauren Nelson and Mark Moccia. "Organizations routinely fund new customer experiences, cloud migrations, platform consolidation, and AI initiatives because leaders can connect them to growth or productivity.

"They are less enthusiastic about updating core systems, simplifying architectures, retiring obsolete components, and eliminating fragile interfaces. The result is a modern front end resting on an aging, brittle, and increasingly interconnected estate."

Forrester's recommendations are to map dependencies, test failures and recovery under realistic conditions, and use incidents and near misses to identify weaknesses before they cause another outage. ®

f823a3b94acced32: WEST PALM BEACH: US President Donald Trump said Thursday he had asked Vladimir Putin to "pull back all military aggression" against Europe, in a fresh shift in tone towards the Russian leader he called his friend just last week.
Trump said he had made the request to Putin when they met in China last week, adding that he thought it would help lead to a deal to end Moscow's grinding war in Ukraine.
Trump's comments come a day after he hosted NATO chief Mark Rutte in Florida, after which the two leaders issued a joint statement calling on Russia not to expand the Ukraine war.

"During my conversations in China with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe,"Trump said on his Truth Social network.
Trump said he had done so "in the hopes that a Deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine, and made quickly."
"I really believe this is a strong possibility – Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, A COMPLETE BLOODBATH – and will be a Great Tribute to everyone!"

The statement did not specify which territories Trump meant – and did not specifically include Ukraine, which Russia invaded in February 2022, kicking off the largest war in Europe since World War II.
But European nations have been increasingly concerned by what they regard as Russian provocations, including three Russian cruise missiles landing in Poland last week.
In their joint statement on Wednesday, Trump and NATO's Rutte said they "discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war."
Trump, who is spending the US Thanksgiving holiday at his Mar-a-Lago resort, reposted the joint statement with Rutte on Truth Social shortly before his new comments on Putin.
In a notable contrast with Trump's recent criticisms of Ukraine for striking targets deep inside Russia, the US leader made no call for Kyiv to show similar restraint.
'DEADLOCK'
Trump's tone appeared markedly different to when Trump met Putin in the Chinese city of Shenzhen last week, both face-to-face and together with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
On that occasion, a smiling Trump welcomed Putin by saying "Who is he? He's my friend," before warmly shaking hands with the Russian leader.
The "friend" comment in particular renewed concerns in Kyiv and European capitals that Trump was once again pivoting towards the Russian leader he has long been close to.

Trump has often appeared more willing to blame Ukraine for Russia's invasion, and has had tense relations with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky since their televised blow-up in the Oval Office in February 2025.
The US envoys on the Ukraine war, Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and business friend Steve Witkoff, have been accused of a similar willingness to take Moscow's side.
In an interview with the German MD Meets Podcast on Wednesday, Kushner said that Putin had "showed restraint" because he had "agreed not to use nuclear weapons."

Kushner also described the Russian leader, whom he has met several times, as a "grandmaster of politics" – while calling the Ukraine conflict "a proxy war where Europe is funding and arming Ukraine against Russia."
But he acknowledged that the issue of territory in eastern Ukraine claimed by Moscow remained a sticking point with Putin.

"What Steve and I have deciphered from having many, many hours with President Putin and from the Russian team, is that you know the territorial issue is right now a little bit of a deadlock," he said.
And he warned against any downward spiral in the Ukraine war, saying it "it won't take a lot of miscalculation for this thing to escalate massively."

0d6305ef5b11368c: HERE'S why many Malaysians lose their shirts to online scammers: they are lulled in, not because they are gullible — though some are — but because modern scams are skilfully engineered to exploit human foibles.
Scammers have found a sweet spot in exploiting trust and fear, routinely using online digital technology to deceive victims.

Take the case of the Johor woman who saw a RM10 maid-booking service as nothing more than a sweet deal — only to find more than RM15,000 surreptitiously drained from her bank account after several attempts to register.
Of course, the RM10 offer on social media was a tantalising bait. Scammers know the bait won't get any bite except from the naive.
Once they manipulated the woman into providing her private banking details, they transferred out her savings to temporary offshore accounts and disappeared for good.
Online fraud has cost Malaysians RM7.33 billion since 2023. About 192,869 complaints were filed until October this year.

While tracking these dastardly schemers is almost impossible, the authorities have made some headway. Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail revealed that 75,266 people were arrested during the same period while 69,665 charges were brought against people linked to 137,699 mule accounts.
Let's get something clear: online transactions and banking are generally safe, provided users exercise care and follow security rules.
But no secure website or transaction can protect a user who carelessly enters banking credentials into a WhatsApp link.
Web security is useless if users install APK files or apps pushed by online sellers.
Banking security collapses the moment users hand over one-time password, transaction authorisation code or banking approval codes.
These are basic precautions, yet most scam victims have, in one way or another, overlooked what is a powerful security force field.
To stay safe, users must check and recheck bank accounts and cellphone numbers through the government's Semak Mule portal as a second line of defence.
Verify any "attractive" online services and offers and do not rely on social media sales pitch.

If money is suddenly siphoned, immediately call the National Scam Response Centre at 997 and alert the relevant bank to freeze access. Finally, lodge a police report. Truth be told, the person on a video call with you may be computer-generated, even if they look and sound like a best friend or close relative.
Scammers are even brazen enough to impersonate officers from the police, Bank Negara Malaysia, Inland Revenue Board, High Court or government agencies.

These days, most deal with these slick scammers by ignoring them or having the intuition to spot the deception. Building experience, education and street savviness to install a mental scam detector may be the strongest psychological defence against ruthless online fraud.

e5f45dd05d13957c: BOLOGNA, Italy: Great Britain booked their place in the semi-finals of the Davis Cup with a 2-1 victory over Alexander Zverev's Germany in Bologna on Thursday.

But that was only good enough to level the tie after Cameron Norrie had seen off Jan-Lennard Struff 6-3 3-6 6-2 in the opening singles.
The tie came down to the doubles which pitted Britain's Henry Patten, the world no.1 in doubles, and Neal Skupski, ranked no.3, against the German pair of Kevin Krawietz and Tim Puetz.
The Britons sailed through the first set 6-2 but had to work harder in the second as it went all the way to a tie-break.
Skupski served for the match at 6-5 but a nervy volley went wide to give the Germans a lifeline. His next serve was clean and gave GB their second match point.
This time a brisk cross-court backhand sealed a 6-2, 7-6 (8/7) victory to send Britain into the semis for the first time in seven years.
"It helps having a guy who can hit a return like that on match point," said Patten. "It makes it a lot easier for me."
Britain, who last won the Davis Cup with Andy Murray in 2015, will face Austria or Spain in Saturday's semi-final.
"We regroup, we relax tomorrow and practise a little bit, and then get ready for whoever we play on Saturday," said Skupski.
Three-time reigning champions Italy will take on the Czech Republic in the first semi on Friday.
3f1d3de01d29fe0e: KUALA LUMPUR: Throughout his more than three decades in the legal profession, former attorney general Tan Sri Abdul Gani Patail played a pivotal role in several high-profile cases that captured public attention, establishing himself as a prominent figure in Malaysia's legal landscape.

Among the high-profile prosecutions Abdul Gani handled were the corruption case involving former Sabah chief minister Datuk Joseph Pairin Kitingan in 1993 and the case involving the Al-Ma'unah militant group in 2000.

The Lahad Datu-born legal figure also led the prosecution team in the case involving 30 individuals, including Philippine nationals, charged with waging war against the Yang di-Pertuan Agong and involvement in various terrorism-related activities in Lahad Datu, Sabah, in 2013.
Abdul Gani, who served as Attorney General for 13 years from 2002 to 2015, died at a private hospital here tonight due to an infection.
Attorney General Tan Sri Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar, who confirmed the news of his death, also extended his condolences to Abdul Gani's family.
"The entire Attorney General's Chambers (AGC) extends its condolences to his family and prays that Allah showers His blessings upon his soul," Mohd Dusuki said when contacted.
Abdul Gani was also part of the prosecution team in the 2006 murder case involving Mongolian national Altantuya Shaariibuu.

He also led the prosecution of former Transport Minister Tun Dr Ling Liong Sik, who was charged in 2010 with cheating the Malaysian government in connection with the Port Klang Free Zone (PKFZ) scandal involving the RM1.08 billion purchase of land in Pulau Indah.
Abdul Gani also handled the prosecution of former Selangor Menteri Besar Dr Mohamad Khir Toyo on corruption charges relating to a property purchase.

He also led the prosecution team in the criminal breach of trust case involving RM76.4 million against former Perwaja Rolling Mill and Development Sdn Bhd managing director Tan Sri Eric Chia Eng Hock and handled the corruption case involving former Land and Cooperative Development Minister Tan Sri Kasitah Gaddam.

Born on Oct 6, 1955, Abdul Gani began his career in the Judicial and Legal Service in 1980 before serving as a deputy public prosecutor at the Attorney General's Chambers in Tawau, Sabah, becoming the first Sabahan to hold the position following the establishment of the federal Attorney General's office in the state.

Throughout his career, he held several key positions, including Sabah head of prosecution in 1991, head of the AGC's Prosecution Division from Jan 16 to Oct 14, 1994, and head and adviser of its International Affairs Division from April 1, 1995, to May 31, 1997.
He subsequently served as Commissioner of Law Revision from 1997 to 2000 before returning as head of the Prosecution Division on Feb 1, 2000.

On Nov 19, 2001, Abdul Gani was appointed Malaysia's eighth Attorney General and officially assumed office on Jan 1, 2002, making history as the first locally trained law graduate to be appointed to the position and the first Sabahan to hold one of the highest posts in the federal civil service.

The appointment marked a major milestone in his legal career, which saw him helm the country's foremost legal institution for more than 13 years before his tenure as Attorney General was terminated on health grounds, effective July 27, 2015.
However, he continued serving as an officer in the Judicial and Legal Service until reaching the mandatory retirement age on Oct 6, 2015.

Abdul Gani also contributed his legal expertise and experience through various other roles, including as a member of the Pardons Board for the Federal Territories of Kuala Lumpur, Labuan and Putrajaya.

He was also appointed an adjunct professor at the Faculty of Law of Universiti Teknologi MARA (UiTM) for two years from Oct 1, 2011, and served as chairman of the National Legal Aid Foundation (YBGK).
On Dec 23, 2016, he was admitted as an advocate and solicitor of the High Court of Malaya. -- BERNAMA

8030417e575dab36: Britain's privacy watchdog is getting a taste of its own medicine, with an independent review set to examine the culture, governance, and accountability surrounding the events that led to former Information Commissioner John Edwards' resignation.
Karon Monaghan KC will examine whether the regulator's culture and governance allowed problems to develop or made concerns harder to raise.

Edwards quit in June after an independent workplace investigation found there was a "case to answer" over his behavior and that his conduct fell short of what was expected of a public official. He disagreed with some of its findings, but ultimately conceded that he had shown "poor judgment."

That investigation, however, focused on Edwards alone. According to the terms of reference published on Thursday, it "did not consider the wider conditions in which that conduct occurred, and it was not designed to."
The new review will cast a wider net. Monaghan wants to know whether staff could call out bad behavior further up the food chain, and what awaited those who tried.

It will also poke around the regulator's leadership and governance arrangements and its relationship with its sponsoring government department, including whether there were adequate ways for concerns to be escalated and those at the top to be challenged.

Current and former staff can give evidence confidentially and voluntarily, while Monaghan will be given access to relevant documents and existing material, including staff surveys and data on bullying, harassment and discrimination.
The ICO has confirmed it won't use confidentiality clauses in settlement agreements to prevent people from contributing to the review.

Monaghan decides which witnesses and documents are relevant, rather than the ICO or DCMS. Access remains subject to legal restrictions, and she must be told when material is withheld and why. She can speak to whoever she thinks is relevant and ask for the complaints, correspondence, and other paperwork she needs.

And if that leads her somewhere unexpected, she can ask to widen the investigation. DCMS can refuse, but it won't be able to quietly brush the request aside, and any decision not to expand the scope has to make it into the final report.
The review won't reopen the investigation into Edwards, make findings about the conduct of named individuals, or delve into the merits of the regulator's enforcement decisions.

Its arrival comes amid a broader shake-up at Britain's data watchdog. The old Information Commissioner's Office was formally replaced by the Information Commission on September 30, bringing with it a new board-led governance model.
The government first promised the wider review in July, shortly after Edwards' departure, but it didn't appoint its reviewer or nail down the terms until late November.
"We need to understand what is working, where things are falling short and, crucially, what needs to change," said DCMS Secretary Lisa Nandy.
The watchdog won't have to wait long for its report card. Monaghan is expected to deliver her findings in the first quarter of 2027, after which they will be published and handed to Parliament. ®

1164219241975555: LONDON: US tobacco group Altria said on Thursday it was considering a possible all-cash offer for Imperial Brands and was in talks with another party over part of the British company's business, as Japan Tobacco also was reported to be weighing a bid.
Shares in London-listed Imperial Brands soared as much as 17.6% to 3,562 pence, giving it a market capitalisation of £26.77 billion (US$35.07 billion).
Bloomberg News earlier on Thursday reported that Japan Tobacco is evaluating a potential acquisition of Imperial Brands, citing people familiar with the matter.
The potential deal comes as the tobacco industry grapples with long-term declines in smoking - its core profit driver - and challenges in building up new revenue streams from alternatives like vapes.

Last week, Imperial Brands, which makes Winston cigarettes, announced plans to cut up to 4,600 jobs, or nearly a fifth of its workforce, as it tightens its grip on costs amid falling cigarette volumes and rising competition.
An Imperial spokesman did not respond to questions on Altria's statement, earlier saying it would never comment on rumour or speculation. Japan Tobacco declined to comment on the report.
Imperial prize

For any buyer, Imperial offers tobacco brands well-known across Europe and the US, with its portfolio including labels like Davidoff, Gauloises and Kool menthol cigarettes sold in more than 100 markets.
A potential deal could mark a return to international cigarette sales for Altria, two decades after it spun off its international division to focus on the US.
That move created Philip Morris International. Altria has not sold cigarettes outside the US since, though it has begun expanding internationally in newer products like nicotine pouches.
Altria has a market value of US$126.89 billion, while Japan Tobacco, which sells brands including Camel and Benson & Hedges in more than 130 markets, is valued at roughly US$69.45 billion.
A deal for Imperial Brands would rank among the largest recent acquisitions of a British company by an overseas buyer.
London-listed firms have become attractive acquisition targets in recent years due to depressed valuations compared to their rivals listed on other European or US exchanges.
Imperial Brands trades at just 8.3 times forward earnings compared with 12.6 times for Altria and 17.7 times for Japan Tobacco, LSEG data showed.
The megadeal adds to this year's global M&A haul, which has been expected by bankers to rival the record-breaking 2021 total even after a pullback in dealmaking in the wake of rising rates.
Searching for growth

Japan Tobacco, Altria and Imperial Brands have all lagged behind rivals such as Philip Morris International and British American Tobacco in building newer product lines, with past efforts by Altria and Imperial to expand beyond traditional tobacco yielding mixed results.
Altria and Japan Tobacco already have ties, having launched a joint venture in 2022 to expand in smoke-free products.

"A joint bid for Imperial from Altria (only present in North America) and Japan Tobacco would neatly swerve anti-trust objections to a possible takeover of Imperial Brands," RBC Capital Markets analyst James Edwardes Jones said in a note.
Altria said it was also in discussions with an unnamed third party for a part of Imperial Brands' business, although no agreement had yet been reached.

Bloomberg News said the Japanese group has been speaking with advisers as it weighs a possible transaction, adding that JT has considered teaming up with a partner to buy Imperial and then split up the British company's assets in different parts of the world.
Under UK takeover rules, Altria has until Dec 24 to make a firm offer for Imperial Brands or walk away.

5474a9739c88ad2e: PETALING JAYA: Ahli perniagaan warga Singapura, Poh Po Lian, berkata cubaan untuk menyingkirkannya sebagai wasi dan pemegang amanah harta pusaka mendiang hartawan Ta Kin Yan menimbulkan kebimbangan serius mengenai motif di sebalik saman tersebut serta sama ada ia bertujuan menggagalkan pentadbiran harta pusaka itu.

Saman tersebut, yang difailkan di Mahkamah Tinggi Kuala Lumpur oleh balu Ta, Lim Chai Yin, pada 10 Nov, memohon geran probet yang diberikan kepada Poh pada 11 Mac lalu dibatalkan mengikut Seksyen 34 Akta Probet dan Pentadbiran.

Lim, yang mendakwa Poh gagal mentadbir harta pusaka itu dengan sewajarnya serta melanggar kewajipan fidusiari sebagai wasi serta pemegang amanah, memohon mahkamah melantik Gan Ah Tee daripada BDO Consulting Sdn Bhd sebagai pentadbir bebas, serta perintah supaya Poh menyerahkan kepada Gan wang milik harta pusaka berkenaan, selain aset dan dokumen.

Dalam kenyataan kepada FMT, firma perhubungan awam yang mewakili Poh mempertikaikan laporan FMT mengenai pertuduhan pecah amanah jenayah yang dihadapinya, sambil menyifatkan tindakan undang-undang 'tidak berasas' itu sebahagian daripada cubaan untuk menyingkirkan Poh dan menghalang beliau daripada melaksanakan tanggungjawab selaras dengan wasiat Ta, geran probet serta undang-undang.
