HongEven before the 2026 midterm elections delivered a clear message about cost-of-living concerns, many states had been raising their minimum wage on their own as one way to increase workers’ purchasing power. And some have taken a more targeted approach, setting wage floors for specific industries. As the example of California shows, however, these initiatives can produce mixed results. In April 2024, California began requiring fast-food chains with at least 60 locations nationwide to pay a minimum wage of US$20 an hour, $4 above the statewide minimum at the time. The governor’s office estimated that more than 500,000 workers would be covered by this mandate. As a researcher of health and labor markets, I joined with economists David Neumark, Gary Wagner and Vitor Melo to run a study measuring the impact on California’s fast-food industry – specifically, whether restaurants employed fewer workers because of the ensuing higher labor costs. We found that the answer depends on which establishments you look at. For the state as a whole, the law didn’t affect employment in any statistically detectable way, we concluded. But smaller chains did take a hit, with employment falling by roughly 20%, while the number of locations dropped by about 10%. New openings fell by 17%-20%, and closures rose by 9%-21%. This employment decline comes almost entirely from fast-food chains ceasing to operate in California, rather than from staffing cuts at the locations that remain. The impact of minimum wage hikes holds importance far beyond the fast-food sector. Their proponents point to the fact that the federal minimum wage of $7.25 an hour has stayed unchanged since 2009 and argue that states and municipalities need to take action on their own. Los Angeles is phasing in a $30 wage for hotel and airport workers, while California’s healthcare workers just received another scheduled increase. Vermont lawmakers have proposed a $20 fast-food wage of their own. In addition, a total of 16 states will raise their minimum wages across the board on Jan. 1, 2027. With the federal minimum wage unchanged since 2009, many states and municipalities have raised the wage floor on their own, including for specific sectors. AP Photo/Andrew Harnik Smaller chains see an impact The question of whether and how minimum wages affect employment still provokes a vigorous debate among economists. In California’s case, some researchers have found that lifting the minimum wage caused small declines in employment compared with other states; others contend that the effect on jobs is essentially zero. More broadly, some researchers have found that minimum wage hikes cost jobs. But the time horizon matters, and effects tend to get larger in the long run. Our study didn’t try to settle that disagreement. Instead, we wanted to find out how employers did adjust, and whether large and small chains responded differently. What happens when higher minimum wages raise one sector’s costs and prices while its closest substitutes – such as sit-down restaurants – keep paying the lower statewide minimum wage? We relied on a database that recorded every business location in the country by name, along with the number of employed workers, each year. That let us directly identify the chains that were subject to California’s law, count each chains’ national footprint to apply the 60-location rule, and track outcomes from 2019 through 2025: total employment, employment at locations that stayed open, the number of locations, and openings and closures. We also compared California with other states and separately compared each chain’s California restaurants with the same chain’s restaurants elsewhere. Finally, we divided the covered chains into two groups: The 20 largest, which account for about 60% of covered jobs, and the 261 smaller ones. For the state as a whole, we found that employment at covered restaurants was basically unchanged, and employment at restaurants that stayed open didn’t change. Among the 20 largest chains, there was no detectable effect at all for any of the measures we tracked over this period. But the smaller chains tell a different story, recording substantial declines in employment, locations and openings, while closures rose. How to reconcile the flat statewide numbers with the sharp effects on smaller chains? The largest chains employ most of the workers affected by the new minimum wage rule, so the statewide total is dominated by them. And the reduced entry and higher exit among smaller chains may have eased competitive pressure on the largest ones. A final point: The biggest chains tend to be the most automated, relying more on equipment such as self-serve kiosks that can reduce the number of workers needed. That may help explain the muted employment response among these larger businesses. Taking the longer view First, we caution that the absence of a clear short-run effect on total employment doesn’t prove that the policy won’t cause bigger job losses over time as companies adapt to the new law. We also can’t answer what happened to the workers at the most affected restaurants or what happened to prices at those establishments, although other research suggests they rose by 3% to 4%. That said, the law was implemented barely 2½ years ago, and some of the larger effects that economists might expect – such as the closure of labor-intensive restaurants or fewer openings – are already apparent among smaller chains. Second, it’s important to remember that California’s fast-food minimum wage applies only to chains with 60 or more locations. So the smaller chains in that range likely lack the scale, automation and pricing power of the national brands and are most sensitive to the new wage floor. Indeed, the law appears to have shifted California’s fast-food market toward its largest chains, a pattern that other researchers documented in a similar study that looked at Germany’s national minimum wage. For the cities and states now weighing wage floors of their own, the California evidence isn’t a slam dunk either way. It shows that the costs, broadly speaking, fall first on the smaller chains covered by the law – but whether it meaningfully impacts the largest chains is unclear. Liam Sigaud is affiliated with the Paragon Health Institute, a not-for-profit health policy research organization.

fb7a1ad02384f987: Amazon said AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server.

The agents were running on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework. The hackers, who provided prompts in simplified Chinese and configured the model to the Chinese Standard Time zone, gave the agents a list of IP addresses and the goal: “obtain shell access.” In short order, the agents discovered a zero-day in an open source medical imaging AI application running on one of the target servers. The agents then exploited the vulnerability and gained full control of the system.
“These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable,” Amazon said.

84edfb5a38475599: One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles. But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report. That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study, his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”
60e8aadceb71593e: From Ann Teoh
Today marks exactly 10 years since Amri Che Mat went missing.
A Suhakam public inquiry unanimously concluded in 2019 that Amri was a victim of enforced disappearance – specifically by state agents, namely the police's Special Branch.
It was past 11pm on Nov 24, 2016, a Thursday, when Amri drove out of his house at Padang Behor in Kangar, Perlis, to have supper with a friend.
Just minutes later, less than a kilometre from his house, his Toyota Fortuner was boxed in by three four-wheel-drives. Screeching sounds, glass breaking, and that was it. It took less than a minute.
Providence would have it that the incident was witnessed by a passing motorcyclist and a restaurant owner across the road from where it happened.

Amri’s Fortuner was found abandoned at a construction site in Bukit Chabang, Kedah, a few hours later. His wife, Norhayati Ariffin, did not realise Amri hadn't come home until the next morning when she received a call about the abandoned car.
Before Amri took a nap at 7.30pm, he had asked his wife to wake him up at 10.30pm. That was the last time Norhayati saw her husband.
This sounds like a bad conspiracy novel, but reality is stranger than fiction.

DNA swabs were taken from the Fortuner when the car was found, but were sent to the chemistry department only five months later. Amri’s family also did not get the police support they wanted. Instead of trying to locate Amri, Norhayati was queried about her husband’s involvement in Shia activities.
Shia Islam is prohibited in Malaysia and Amri was watched by religious authorities and the police, but was never arrested or charged. Instead, he disappeared.
How do we know Amri was being watched? Would he have disappeared at a different time if he didn’t go out that fateful night? It's quite possible judging by the circumstances.
A car workshop owner across Amri’s house later testified that unknown cars, with engines running, took turns parking outside Amri's house day and night for three days before he went missing.
One of those cars was a gold-coloured Toyota Vios with a Penang number plate, which was also spotted when Pastor Raymond Koh was abducted 81 days later.

The Vios belonged to an operative of the Special Branch in Kuala Lumpur. He was identified as Saiful Bahari Abdul Aziz, but the police always had an excuse for why the key witness could not be present to testify.
Koh was abducted the same way on Feb 13, 2017. His car was also boxed in as men in black rushed out from three black four-wheel-drives. There was also a gold-coloured Vios nearby.

Koh’s abduction was more audacious than Amri’s; it happened in broad daylight on a Monday morning in SS4, Petaling Jaya. Amri’s case only had eyewitness accounts but Koh's case included video evidence.
Besides witness Roeshan Celestine Gomez, a chambering student who happened to be driving behind Koh's car, the pastor's abduction was caught on the CCTV cameras of two houses nearby.

Strangely, the police didn’t rush to get the CCTV recordings. It was Koh’s family who looked for them once they knew about Roeshan’s police report. After the CCTV recordings were spread through the media, the case couldn't be hidden any longer.

With two Malaysians abducted this way – and Joshua Helmi and Ruth Sitepu also missing since end-November 2016 – and a growing suspicion they were abducted, a group of civil society groups sent a memo to Suhakam seeking action.

Suhakam then carried out public inquiries on both Koh and Amri’s disappearances. Amri’s case took Suhakam 10 months to complete starting from January 2018, with 27 days of hearings and 24 witnesses summoned.

Suhakam's final reports said evidence pointed to Amri and Koh being forcibly abducted by the Special Branch. It also stated that in both cases, the police failed to investigate the disappearances properly.

The Cabinet then set up a special task force in 2019 to look into the matter. Its report in 2020 stated that it was “highly probable that Amri’s disappearance was caused by rogue police officers acting alone or in a group with unidentified individuals from religious groups".

Three years after Amri disappeared, Norhayati, who became a single mother to their four daughters, sued the police and government for malfeasance and failure to investigate his abduction properly, among others.

The civil suit filed on Nov 18, 2019, took six years, partly because the government initially refused to release the special task force's report. By the time the High Court made its decision, nine years had passed since Amri disappeared.

On Nov 5, 2025, the High Court awarded Norhayati general and exemplary damages totalling RM3 million, and another RM14,457.52 mainly for the children’s education expenses. The court also ordered a re-investigation into Amri’s disappearance.

Justice Su Tiang Joo said the police breached their own SOPs, citing severe delays in handling DNA evidence, failure to investigate the Vios owner, and failure to investigate CCTV recordings, among others. The police also made almost no effort to keep the family updated.

Su said Norhayati’s mental anguish, pain and suffering included having to dissolve her marriage under fasakh – as advised by the Perlis religious affairs department – “to bring succour to the needs of the four daughters".

Norhayati was unable to get welfare aid as a single mother if she remained married to Amri. Secondly, the divorce dispensed of the need for Amri to be a wali for one of their daughters who was getting married.
Perhaps it was to be expected that the attorney-general would appeal the High Court decision. With that, the award was stayed while Norhayati and her daughters continue to wait.
Today, we want to remember Amri.
Whatever wrongs he allegedly committed, Amri deserves a fair chance at defending himself in a court of law.
That’s the basic minimum of a modern democratic society proclaiming the supremacy of the constitution and rule of law as two of its five Rukun Negara tenets.

Abducting Amri was cowardly and dastardly because the government has the machinery, laws, institutions and manpower resources to frame a legal case against him and prosecute him, if he indeed did wrong.
The police chose a shortcut instead, and the executive arm of the government allowed that shortcut. This was a betrayal of the rakyat's trust.
Today, we remember Amri Che Mat, a Malaysian, a father of four girls (now grown women), and surely, a friend to many through his NGO, Perlis Hope.
Ann Teoh is an FMT reader.

9c8bf06abbbe421e: Complaints include marriage disputes, unfair trial, unlawful land grabs, corruption, torture, and more
Originally published on Global Voices
An old man in the Talas province addressing Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov during a public meeting. Photo from the Presidential Administration's website. Fair Use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In October and November 2026, Kyrgyzstan’s president, Sadyr Japarov, held public meetings with the population in all seven provinces of the country. What were meant to be formal events turned into quests for justice by people driven to desperation.
The meetings revealed the ineffectiveness of the existing justice mechanisms and showed how people saw the president as the only guarantor of justice.

The effectiveness of Kyrgyzstan’s law enforcement and judicial bodies was people’s most common justice-related complaint. During a meeting with residents of the southwestern Batken province on October 11, a woman complained to the president about her former husband, who accused her of forging their marriage certificate and framed her for crimes she did not commit to avoid the division of assets after their divorce.

She also said her former brother-in-law provided false testimony to back up his brother’s accusations. She now lives in an apartment with their three children in constant fear that her former husband may kick them out because he allegedly bribed police and courts.

This trivial legal dispute reached the point where the woman had to beg the president to ensure a just investigation and ruling. Japarov condemned her former husband and said that he should have left everything to her and their kids after the divorce.
Here is an Instagram reel with his response to the case.
View this post on Instagram

On October 26, Japarov met with residents of the Kazarman district in the southern Jalalabad province, where Shirimbek Abrahmanov told the president about his father, who was imprisoned for allegedly offering a bribe of KGS 2,000 (USD 23) to a police officer during a traffic stop. The district court acquitted him of the charges.
However, the local prosecutor’s office appealed the decision in the provincial court, which found Abdrahmanov’s father guilty and sentenced him to two years in prison.
Here is an Instagram reel with the complaint and Japarov’s response.
View this post on Instagram
Japarov could not hide his anger when he heard the story, especially after finding out the provincial court took seven months to issue a verdict. In reply, he confronted local authorities and said:

Are the traffic police officer and the prosecutor in cahoots? Does that mean they’ve ganged up on him? If it were a large bribe, that would be one thing. But to have someone imprisoned over two thousand soms — that’s a disgrace.
The man was released from custody shortly after Japarov’s intervention and subsequent pardon.
Similar complaints resurfaced multiple times during presidential meetings in other provinces, highlighting systemic problems plaguing the judicial and law-enforcement systems.
The message is clear: people have lost all hope of finding justice at the hands of local police and courts.

Surprisingly, following his meetings with the public, Japarov concluded that the level of distrust towards courts has decreased, but admitted that problems in the judicial system remain and must be solved quickly.

On the one hand, the lack of justice and the dysfunction within the courts and police bodies, which are plagued by corruption and bureaucracy, are real pressing issues affecting millions of people across Kyrgyzstan. However, the current political regime led by Japarov, who came to power in October 2020, has made little tangible progress.
In 2026, Kyrgyzstan was ranked 99th out of 144 states in the Rule of Law Index compiled by the World Justice Project. For comparison, in 2020, it was ranked 87th.

On the other hand, people’s desperate appeals for justice helped Japarov sustain his man-of-the-people image. By listening to people’s requests and swiftly resolving their issues, the president can reinforce his popularity. In turn, this leads to the maintenance of the personalistic regime built around Japarov since his arrival to power.

Nikos Oikonomou/Anadolu via Getty ImagesThe International Court of Justice (ICJ) last week ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority group. The court found Myanmar breached its obligations under the United Nations genocide convention to prevent and punish genocide. This ruling is not just important for the Rohingya and Myanmar. It may also have a significant legal impact on other genocide cases before the court – in particular, South Africa’s case alleging Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. Other genocide cases Four cases currently before the ICJ concern allegations of breaches of the genocide convention. One was brought by Ukraine against Russia following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Another was brought by Nicaragua against Germany, regarding Germany’s support of Israel’s actions in Gaza. The third was brought by the Democratic Republic of Congo against Rwanda, which includes claims about Rwanda’s involvement in conflict in the Kivu provinces of the DRC. The Myanmar ruling may have repercussions for all these cases. However, the judgement will mostly affect the fourth genocide case before the court, the one brought by South Africa against Israel. Multiple intents Genocide is different from “ordinary” crimes in that it requires a “special intent” (or dolus specialis) – the intent to destroy a national, racial, ethnic or religious group, in whole or in part. This must be proven in addition to a general criminal intent, where a perpetrator intends to commit the crime or could have foreseen the result of their actions. Genocidal intent is proven by two main forms of evidence. Firstly, there are the statements of political and military leaders, soldiers, the media and key figures in society. These often dehumanise the targeted group and may explicitly refer to the destruction of the group in some way. The second way intent is proven is by looking at the perpetrators’ pattern of conduct. In the Myanmar case, the court considered hate speech by Myanmar authorities against the Rohingya to be incitement to genocide. This formed evidence of intent. The judges also used the military’s pattern of conduct to determine intent. Myanmar argued its intent was a counterinsurgency operation against a terrorist group, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA). But the court determined the conduct of Myanmar’s security forces did not align with an intent to carry out a genuine counterinsurgency operation. The court held that acts such killing civilians (including children), raping women, and destroying villages did not form part of legitimate military operations – even if the operation also had the intent of meeting military objectives. This is significant for the Israel genocide case because Israel argues it is fighting in self-defence in Gaza against a terrorist group, Hamas. However, statements from Israeli government ministers about the intention to deny Palestinians necessities of life, or to erase Palestine from the map, may suggest a different intent. As in the Myanmar case, the violence in Gaza has included the killing of civilians (including children), the widespread destruction of buildings (including in residential areas), and sexual and gender-based violence. The Myanmar judgement gives the court an opening to decide that Israel has had both an intent to fight Hamas and a genocidal intent. Or it could decide Israel’s operations in Gaza do not represent a legitimate and lawful way to carry out an anti-terrorism military operation, which may demonstrate clear genocidal intent. Killing of children One of the key aspects of The Gambia’s case against Myanmar was that the killing of children demonstrated genocidal intent. The reason: killing children is not a legitimate military objective. The ICJ agreed. The court held that the killing of up to 2,000 children under the age of five was a significant indicator that Myanmar intended to destroy the future of the Rohingya people. According to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, Israel has killed almost 22,000 children under 18 in Gaza. Some have been killed in indiscriminate attacks. Others have been deliberately targeted, according to the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel. Following the court’s Myanmar decision, the killing of so many children in Gaza may strengthen the case against a legitimate military operation, and that the military and therefore the state instead had genocidal intent. Broader context of crimes The Myanmar cased focused on the so-called “clearance operations” against the Rohingya in 2017. However, this violence was placed in the context of a lengthy history of discrimination and persecution of the Rohingya. The court recognised that violations of human rights, which may not necessarily amount to genocidal crimes, were part of the bigger picture of the genocide. The exclusion of the Rohingya from citizenship was one example, as it denied them access to education, employment, healthcare, food and free movement. Similarly, South Africa’s case against Israel positions the violence in Gaza since 2023 as an escalating step in decades of discrimination and persecution – a system of apartheid – against Palestinians. Scale and targeting of crimes ICJ judges also recognised that the scale of the crimes in Myanmar was relevant to the finding that genocide occurred, alongside the fact the violence specifically targeted the Rohingya. Thousands of Rohingya were killed and raped, and myriad Rohingya villages were destroyed. Non-Rohingya were not attacked, and their villages were not burned. This has parallels to the situation in Gaza. Large numbers of Palestinians have been killed and injured, and huge swathes of Gaza have been destroyed. It is estimated it will take many years and billions of dollars to clear and rebuild Gaza. These findings have clear parallels with the situation in Gaza, and will undoubtedly be drawn on by South Africa as its case against Israel progresses in the coming years. d72fc07dea2532a0: Hari itu Ahmad Maslan berpantun di Dewan Rakyat. Selain terkenal dengan resipi nasi gorengnya, Timbalan menteri kerja raya itu memang gemar berpantun. Tapi, bukan tentang kenapa dan apa sebab beliau berpantun yang ingin saya ceritakan. Tolak ke tepi bab politik, saya rasa ada sesuatu yang wajar kita hargai daripada kegemaran beliau itu. Bagi saya pantun perlu diangkat sebagai pusaka negara dan mesti diajar dengan serius di sekolah ketika kita mencari formula lain dalam usaha menggalakkan pelajar berfikir secara kritis dan kreatif.

Pantun mampu mengasah kemahiran tersebut. Hari ini tak ramai orang mampu berpantun secara spontan. Kalau diberikan pen dan kertas serta masa setengah jam, mungkin ramai yang boleh menghasilkan pantun empat kerat. Itupun pantun yang asal boleh sajalah! Bukan pantun yang betul-betul bermutu tinggi. Tetapi bagaimana jika kita perlu melakukannya dalam masa beberapa saat atau membalas pantun secara spontan? Saya percaya kita memang gagal. Di situlah menariknya pantun sebagai penajam akal.

Kita selalu membicarakan pantun sebagai warisan kesusasteraan Melayu. Tetapi jarang sekali kita membicarakannya dari sudut keupayaan kognitif manusia. Bagi saya, pantun bukan sekadar permainan bahasa, tetapi juga suatu bentuk latihan ketangkasan berfikir. Bayangkan apa yang berlaku dalam kepala seseorang ketika mencipta pantun secara spontan. Kita perlu memikirkan perkara yang hendak disampaikan, mencari perkataan yang sesuai, menyusun ayat, memadankan rima serta membina pembayang. Semua itu dilakukan hampir serentak. Belum lagi kalau pantun itu perlu dijawab apabila ada yang menjualnya.

Otak perlu bekerja untuk memahami maksud yang disampaikan oleh orang lain, merumuskan jawapan dan menterjemahkan jawapan itu dalam bentuk puisi yang mempunyai peraturan tertentu. Ini bukan mudah. Cuma, selama ini kita lihat pantun seolah-olah dipermainkan dan dijadikan bahan lawak sahaja dalam rancangan hiburan atau persembahan komedi. Kita kena serius sekali-sekala.

Dalam bidang pendidikan, kita sering bercakap tentang pemikiran kritis. Kita mahu anak-anak kita mempunyai kemampuan menganalisis, mentafsir, membuat perkaitan dan menyelesaikan masalah secara kreatif. Menariknya, sebahagian daripada kemahiran berfikir itu sudah lama dilatih oleh nenek moyang kita melalui suatu kegiatan yang hari ini sering kita anggap sekadar hiburan.

Bukanlah bermaksud syarat hendak berpantun mestilah mempunyai pemikiran kritis yang tinggi. Tetapi proses mencipta pantun itu sendiri memerlukan beberapa kemahiran mental yang amat berguna dalam membentuk pemikiran seseorang. Pantun juga ada tingkatannya. Ada pantun yang mudah, sekadar memadankan bunyi di hujung baris. Ada pula pantun yang pembayangnya mempunyai hubungan makna dengan maksud yang hendak disampaikan. Lebih tinggi lagi apabila pencipta pantun menggunakan perlambangan alam untuk menyampaikan falsafah kehidupan. Contohnya pantun ini:-
Yang kurik itu kundi, Yang merah itu saga; Yang baik itu budi, Yang indah itu bahasa.

Betapa ekonomisnya penggunaan bahasa dalam menyampaikan suatu pemikiran. Tak perlu panjang berjela, empat baris sahaja sudah cukup untuk membicarakan nilai kemanusiaan. Orang Melayu dahulu memerhatikan alam. Mereka melihat tumbuh-tumbuhan, haiwan, sungai, laut dan perubahan cuaca. Daripada pemerhatian itu, mereka membina perlambangan dan menghubungkannya dengan kehidupan manusia. Ini bukan sekadar persoalan penguasaan bahasa. Ini juga persoalan keupayaan membuat perkaitan antara dua perkara yang pada zahirnya kelihatan tidak mempunyai hubungan. Kemampuan membuat perkaitan inilah yang dimaksudkan sebagai salah satu ciri pemikiran kreatif.

Menteri pendidikan patut beri perhatian yang serius akan kemahiran yang sudah lama kita miliki ini. Pantun bukan sekadar diajar sebagai salah satu bentuk puisi tradisional dalam mata pelajaran bahasa Melayu semata-mata tetapi dijadikan kegiatan yang melatih anak-anak berfikir secara spontan. Adakan sesi jual beli pantun di dalam kelas. Seorang pelajar mengemukakan persoalan dalam bentuk pantun dan seorang lagi menjawabnya juga dalam bentuk pantun. Biarkan mereka belajar sambil berseronok walaupun pada permulaannya mungkin mutu pantun masih rendah. Lama-kelamaan sudah tentu pelajar akan jadi mahir serta tangkas seperti pantun lama ini:
Limau purut lebat di pangkal, Batang mengkudu condong uratnya; Hujan ribut dapat ditangkal, Hati yang rindu apa ubatnya?

Perhatikan kehalusannya. Jika anak-anak kita mampu mencipta pantun sebegini bermakna mereka telah memahami falsafah hubungan perasaan manusia dengan fenomena alam. Hujan ribut yang dahsyat sekalipun masih dianggap mampu ditangkal, tetapi kerinduan yang tidak kelihatan itu belum tentu mampu diubati.

Bayangkan juga jika seorang guru sains meminta anak muridnya menerangkan sesuatu konsep sains melalui pantun. Sudahlah perlu memahami konsep itu, mereka perlu pula memikirkan cara menyampaikannya dalam empat baris. Tentulah ada yang secara sinis mempersoalkan mengapa perlu menyusahkan diri sedangkan penerangan biasa lebih mudah. Inilah yang saya maksudkan sejak awal lagi ia bertujuan untuk mencabar kemampuan minda. Contoh lucunya ialah mamat-mamat sado yang mengangkat besi di gimnasium pun boleh kita tanyakan soalan yang sama. Mengapa bersusah payah mengangkat besi berat sebab lepas itu letak semula besi tersebut di tempat asalnya. Tapi kita segera faham yang dia sedang melatih ototnya, manakala orang yang berpantun pula sedang melatih akalnya.

Dalam zaman kecerdasan buatan hari ini, kita boleh meminta komputer menghasilkan puluhan pantun dalam beberapa saat. Tetapi tujuan mengajar anak-anak berpantun bukanlah semata-mata untuk mendapatkan pantun yang indah. Yang lebih penting ialah proses mental yang dilalui untuk menghasilkan pantun tersebut. Kita tidak mahu sekadar melahirkan generasi yang tahu mendapatkan jawapan. Kita juga mahu melahirkan generasi yang tahu bagaimana hendak berfikir untuk mendapatkan jawapan. Bertuahnya kita ialah kita sudah ada kaedah yang praktikal dalam hal ini tetapi kita kesampingkannya. Orang tua kita dulu apabila berpantun macam, GhatGpt. Prompt saja terus keluar jawapan.

Satu lagi keistimewaan pantun ialah kemampuannya menyampaikan teguran secara halus. Orang boleh berselisih pendapat, menyindir, menegur, malah berbahas tanpa semestinya menggunakan bahasa yang kasar. Dalam zaman manusia begitu mudah memaki hamun di media sosial, alangkah menariknya jika mereka perlu berpantun dahulu sebelum mahu bergaduh. Sekurang-kurangnya ada tapisan sedikit sebelum menghina orang. Kedengaran mungkin lucu, tapi kita lihatlah hari ini berapa ramai mengalami kemurungan akibat dimaki hamun di media sosial. Barangkali ada yang akan membatalkan hasrat untuk bergaduh kerana terlalu sibuk mencari pembayang. Lihatlah ketika Ahmad Maslan berpantun. Bunyinya tenang sahaja tetapi 'makan dalam'. Berbanding beberapa Ahli Parlimen yang gemar menjerit dan bertempik sehingga penyokong sendiri pun naik malu.

Kita patut berbangga dengan warisan budaya kita. Namun, kebanggaan itu tidak seharusnya terhenti pada usaha memelihara bentuknya semata-mata. Kita juga harus menggali kebijaksanaan di sebalik penciptaannya dan mencari bagaimana ia boleh dimanfaatkan dalam kehidupan moden. Pantun bukan sekadar khazanah bahasa. Ia juga khazanah pemikiran. Nenek moyang kita bukan sahaja mewariskan keindahan berbahasa, malah suatu kaedah untuk melatih ketangkasan akal.

Kalau kita sendiri kurang menghargai keistimewaan pantun, tahukah kita bahawa hampir dua abad dahulu sasterawan Perancis sudah tertarik dengannya? Pada tahun 1829, Victor Hugo, pengarang Les Misérables, memperkenalkan pantun berkait Melayu menerusi antologi puisinya, Les Orientales. Bentuk puisi ini kemudian diadaptasi oleh penyair Perancis sehingga dikenali sebagai pantoum.

Bayangkan, ketika orang Eropah sedang meneroka keunikan struktur puisi warisan kita, nenek moyang kita sudah menjadikannya sebahagian daripada cara mereka berkomunikasi dalam kehidupan seharian. Sayang sekali jika kita hanya mewarisi pantunnya tetapi tidak mewarisi kecerdasan berfikir yang melahirkan pantun itu. Dan dalam bab ini, saya menghargai kegemaran Ahmad Maslan berpantun. Agak-agak bernas atau tidak cadangan saya agar kemahiran berpantun diajar secara serius di sekolah?

97bbc033a9e9fa11: A president’s absence and a president’s disqualification are two different things. Malaysia Athletics must establish what its constitution requires when an incumbent becomes ineligible to hold office.
World Athletics has disqualified Karim Ibrahim. He has not appealed against the decision, and the international governing body has not lifted the sanction.

Article 13.2.8 of Malaysia Athletics’ endorsed constitution sets out the consequence. It makes a person ineligible to be nominated, elected, appointed or hold office if he has been disqualified, removed or suspended by Malaysia Athletics, the Olympic Council of Malaysia, the Asian Athletics Association, World Athletics or another local or international sports authority or organisation.
That ineligibility continues until the relevant authority releases the person from the sanction or he succeeds in an appeal.
Karim’s disqualification therefore makes him ineligible to hold office under this provision. Malaysia Athletics must formally record it and address the consequences for the presidency.
The issue now is not the existence of the sanction, but how the association applies its own constitution to the leadership position it has affected.
The deputy president’s authority needs a clear basis
Malaysia Athletics deputy president Wan Hisham Wan Salleh now regards himself as the acting president. But the constitution must provide a sound basis for that position.

Article 12.2.2 allows the deputy president to chair Malaysia Athletics meetings when the president is absent. It also allows him to assume the president’s rights and duties at those meetings, as designated by the president.
The clause deals with the president’s absence. It does not expressly state that the deputy president automatically becomes acting president when the incumbent is disqualified from holding office.
Nor does it spell out how the deputy president should assume the full responsibilities of the presidency in those circumstances.
That difference cannot be brushed aside.

A president who is away or unable to attend a meeting may still hold office. Disqualification raises a different issue: the incumbent is no longer eligible to occupy the position under Article 13.2.8.
Wan Hisham’s claim to be acting president therefore needs more than an assumption that the deputy president naturally takes over.
The council must identify the constitutional provision, decision or other valid authority that supports his position.

Article 12.2.2 may provide for the deputy president to perform certain duties during the president’s absence. But the wording supplied does not, by itself, establish an automatic succession process after disqualification.
It also does not expressly give the deputy president a mandate to serve as acting president until the next election.
This is where the executive council must do its work. Article 18.1 gives it sole authority to interpret the association’s constitution and by-laws.
It must examine the relevant provisions together, determine what they require and record its decision.

That interpretive power does not allow the council to create a succession rule that the constitution does not contain. It must apply the written provisions, not stretch them to fit an administrative arrangement.
The council should examine Article 12.2.2 alongside Article 13.2.8 and any other clauses dealing with vacancies, removal from office, an acting president or fresh elections.
If another provision sets out the succession process, the council must follow it. If the constitution leaves the position unclear, it should obtain legal advice before deciding how to proceed.
Wan Hisham has said he will brief the executive council at its Nov 29 meeting. He has declined to answer legal and constitutional questions while awaiting legal advice.
The meeting offers the council a timely opportunity to consider the disqualification, clarify the authority under which the association is operating and decide the next steps.
It should leave no doubt about who holds the presidency, what powers that person may exercise and which constitutional provisions support the arrangement.
Other decisions need scrutiny, not sweeping conclusions
The council must also consider whether Karim’s disqualification affects decisions and appointments made during his time in office.
It should not assume that every decision made under his leadership is now invalid. Equally, it should not treat every appointment as beyond question.
Each case requires a review of the relevant eligibility rules, appointment process and circumstances.

The same care applies to the annual general meeting and the election of office-bearers. Karim’s disqualification does not, by itself, invalidate the entire meeting or the positions of everyone elected.
Any challenge must rest on the relevant constitutional provisions and the facts surrounding the election.
Members may also ask whether they can table a motion of no confidence in the current leadership.
The constitution’s provisions on notice, meetings, voting and removal must determine whether they can do so and what effect such a motion would have.
A vote of no confidence does not necessarily remove an office-bearer unless the rules provide for it.
The council should answer these questions by referring to the constitution, not through informal assurances or political agreement.
Members need to know which rules apply and how the association intends to enforce them.
Malaysia Athletics cannot afford further uncertainty over who has authority to lead it and where that authority comes from.
The association must record Karim’s disqualification, establish the status of the presidency and identify the proper process for filling the position.
It must also clarify the deputy president’s powers while that process unfolds.

If the constitution requires an election, the association should follow the prescribed procedure. If it provides another route, the council should explain and apply it. Either way, members must be able to trace the decision to a clear constitutional provision.

This is not a contest between Karim and Wan Hisham, or an opportunity for one faction to gain an advantage over another. It is a test of whether Malaysia Athletics can govern by rules rather than assumptions.
The executive council has the authority to interpret the constitution. It also has a duty to apply it fairly, consistently and transparently.
A constitution cannot be stretched to suit the people who happen to hold office. It exists to govern them, especially when leadership is in dispute. The Nov 29 meeting should make that clear.

972640f78a70025d: On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children.

SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM).

Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked. Although X Safety and xAI (now known as SpaceXSI) were silent at first, Musk’s companies eventually apologized and claimed that additional safeguards were implemented and policies redesigned to block harmful outputs. However, state attorneys general alleged that those statements were “misleading” and that SpaceXSI instead quietly “embraced” sexualized content to seize more AI market share, as Grok continues to generate NCII and CSAM today.
f82e2058d3bb9c30: Languages take on thousands of forms. Some are tonal, like Vietnamese, where shifts in pitch convey distinct meanings. English relies on precise word orders, but this matters less for Russian, where words can be swapped without changing the intended message.  Despite so much variety in the linguistic kingdom, an MIT study has found that the human brain may process all sorts of languages in a universal way. Artificial intelligence made this finding possible. In the study published today in Nature Neuroscience, the researchers used multilingual models to predict how the human brain responds to various languages. Those models also helped the researchers detect a shared brain process across people who collectively spoke 21 different languages. “Of course, there are many differences in the ways humans converse with each other. But our team found that there is something fundamentally similar in how the brain communicates,” says Evelina Fedorenko, who is an investigator at MIT’s McGovern Institute for Brain Research, an associate professor of brain and cognitive sciences, and the senior author of the paper. The study is the first to use multilingual models to predict brain responses across many languages. As researchers develop AI language tools to diagnose brain disorders, this work can extend their benefit to speakers of more languages, and may one day even keep endangered ones from vanishing. Parsing the linguistic mind Language allows us to share our thoughts about the outside world and the ones we create in our minds. That power lives within a network of brain regions located in the left hemisphere. “Every language is managed by these same parts of the brain,” explains Andrea Gregor de Varda, the lead author of the new study, a postdoc in the Fedorenko lab, and fellow in the K. Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center. While scientists know that all languages activate the same parts of the brain, de Varda and Fedorenko wanted to know if that meant the brain processes them in the same way. For example, they wondered, does the brain of someone who speaks Korean operate comparably to the brains of a Hindi or Spanish speaker? It’s extremely hard to answer that question if you lack the right tools, de Varda says. And they needed one capable of creating a common code for comparing all sorts of languages — a task that is well-suited to artificial intelligence. Where AI meets the brain Large language models (LLMs) — such as those powering ChatGPT and Claude — interpret language much like the human brain, although they weren’t designed to do so. That surprising similarity is allowing de Varda and others in the field to wield these tools as a piercing lens into the human mind. Such studies often explore LLMs’ ability to learn or make sense of linguistic elements, such as grammar and meaning, to glean insights into how the brain might handle communication. But early LLMs used to work within a single language. The MIT researchers thought another class of models might help expand that scope. “Multilingual language models are LLMs that can process hundreds of languages at once,” explains Fedorenko. Like other AIs of their kind, multilingual models ingest words or phrases and output numbers that scientists can extract. “Those numbers show how the model represents that bit of language,” she says. Now the team could study many languages at once using a single numerical code from the models. But the extent to which the models aligned with the human mind still lurked in the unknowns. De Varda believed he could coax an answer into light through a computational approach. Using machine learning, he merged two data sources: the multilingual models’ code and scans of people’s brains as they performed linguistic tasks. The product was an AI tool known as an encoding model. It takes a multilingual model’s code, say, for a sentence, and predicts how the human brain might light up in response to the same input. Encoding models at the time only existed for a handful of languages including English, French, and Chinese. But de Varda sought to test whether those models could be extended to more — and importantly, understudied ones. Doing so could reveal new aspects in which AI mirrors the human brain, and even detect a shared neural component across speakers of various languages. A mental bridge between languages The Fedorenko lab already had preexisting brain imaging data from speakers of 12 languages: Afrikaans, Dutch, Farsi, French, Lithuanian, Marathi, Norwegian, Romanian, Spanish, Tamil, Turkish, and Vietnamese. They recruited speakers of nine additional ones for their new study — Italian, Portuguese, German, Russian, Polish, Hindi, Arabic, Mandarin, and Korean — and recorded their brain activity while they listened to stories from “Alice in Wonderland” in their native language. By coupling that brain imaging data with outputs from multilingual models, the team created encoding models for those 21 languages. “We found that the encoding models accurately predicted brain responses in all of the languages we studied — even in Marathi and Lithuanian, that, in contrast to English, we only have a limited amount of data on,” says Fedorenko. “The fact that there’s this emergent similarity between models and humans across so many languages is really quite exciting.” Another finding was more interesting still. Even though the researchers trained an encoding model in a single language, it could predict brain activity for a language it had never seen before. For example, an encoding model trained to predict brain responses in French could also predict responses in Vietnamese, without ever being trained in Vietnamese. It was a truly fascinating discovery, de Varda says, because this was only possible if all the speakers’ brains were representing language in a shared way: a neural thread binding human communication. What was that shared component? Dissecting different linguistic features across all the languages suggested that it has something to do with meaning. “That’s the intended power of communication, right? To share meaning; new information or our feelings about the world. So it’s fascinating we see that reflected in this work,” says Fedorenko. In science, this new study gives brain researchers some explanations for long-held curiosities among them. In society, it could steer emerging technologies into a more inclusive direction. Scientists are starting to explore clinical uses of AI language tools, such as those that can detect cognitive decline based on brain activity patterns during language. But most of those studies, and the methods clinicians use today, are in common and well-studied languages like English. By showing how AI and the human brain overlap across many diverse languages, this new research may be a step toward clinical tools that do not leave most speakers out. In another vein, reversing the Fedorenko lab’s approach might help preserve languages on the brink of extinction. “Say you had one single speaker of a language that is dying out. You might imagine a case in which we can train a model in the opposite direction: give it images of that speaker’s brain, and it could translate those into language,” notes Fedorenko. De Varda adds that there are features that clearly differ between languages, too, and that those must be somehow represented in the brain and even LLMs. Defining those differences in future research, he says, might unearth new fragments of knowledge to complete the puzzle of the linguistic mind.
1e8d527100dd7796: On Nov. 22, the day after COP31 climate talks collapsed in Antalya, Turkey, the global average temperature at noon UTC was estimated to be a record-setting 2.36 C above the pre-industrial average. Climate change is driving up global temperatures. Yet governments could not even agree to name the fossil fuels driving it. I have been a climate scientist since the late 1980s and have followed every UN climate summit since the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. I cannot recall a more embarrassing failure than COP31. The first draft proposed at least US$120 billion by 2035 to help countries adapt to climate change. By Nov. 19, the figure was gone. Three years ago in Dubai, governments agreed to transition away from fossil fuels. The Nov. 16 Antalya draft said so plainly. Yet, the final proposal at COP31 still omitted any mention of fossil fuels. The European Union and small island states were right to reject it. Given the recent failure, is it time for scientists and activists to boycott COP? From early success to utter failure While COP31 collapsed without an agreement, previous UN climate talks have had successes. In the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, industrialized countries agreed to reduce their collective emissions, averaged over 2008–12, to 5.2 per cent below 1990 levels. Emissions over the 2008-12 reporting period came in 9.9 per cent below 1990 levels. In Paris in 2015, governments agreed to hold warming “well below 2 C above pre-industrial levels” while “pursuing efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5 C above pre-industrial levels.” Yet, in June 2026, a UN report found that the world is set to exceed the 1.5 C global warming target outlined in Paris. In 2015, governments invited the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) to report back in 2018 on the impacts of 1.5 C of warming and the emissions pathways that could get us there. In future emissions pathways leading to little or no overshoot of the 1.5 C target, global net carbon dioxide emissions were required to fall roughly 45 per cent from 2010 levels by 2030 and reach net zero around 2050. Those pathways also required removing 100 to 1,000 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere over the century (so-called negative emissions) using technology that had yet to be developed. The authors spelled out the difficulties. The key government takeaway was that meeting the 1.5 C target could still be achieved. What struck me was how little those models resembled the world in which people make decisions. You can write carbon removal into a model. Somebody still has to find the land, build the equipment and pay to operate it. You don’t build a coal plant today to tear it down tomorrow. The utility has debt to repay and communities need power. What if we stayed home? Andrew Weaver on BBC News discussing COP31. Scientists, environmentalists and youth groups should boycott the next COP. I further think scientists should also consider walking away from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change assessments. I was a lead author on four of them. I know what that invitation means to a young scientist, yet at some point, the scientific community needs to speak out as a collective. And those of us who have already had the privilege of working on IPCC assessments ought to speak first — and loudest. The Paris Agreement showed how readily governments can use our willingness to buy time. Ministers agreed on a temperature, asked us what it would mean if the world exceeded it, then continued exploiting fossil fuels regardless. Climate change has become a global tragedy of the commons. Fossil-fuel producers earn money selling their products while sharing the climatic cost with everyone else. Countries and tech companies are incentivized to race ahead with artificial intelligence, regardless of the environmental risks the rest of us inherit. And in our politics, climate change has become subsumed into a culture war where politics rail against green policies regardless of the facts. While Canada’s delegates were in Antalya, Ottawa committed $200 million to expand planned production at Woodfibre LNG, a liquefied natural gas export terminal in British Columbia. With decisions like that, the world is on course to even exceed 2 C of global warming. So, let governments go to the next COP and explain the empty seats. Save the airfare, the emissions and two weeks of time better spent elsewhere. Instead, use a fraction of that time to ask your representatives about the tangible action they are taking to tackle climate change. Andrew Weaver receives funding from NSERC and NRCan. He has previously served as an MLA and leader of the BC Green Party.
9cbcfc27624697ca: In a 2019 referendum, close to 98% of Bougainvilleans for independence. After more than a century of struggle, Bougainville is moving closer to becoming the world’s newest nation. An autonomous region of Papua New Guinea (PNG) in the northern Solomon Islands chain, Bougainville is taking its next step toward self-determination after a decade-long civil war and a 25-year peace process. In a 2019 referendum, almost 98% of Bougainvilleans voted for independence. Today the parliament of PNG will begin to vote on ratifying that result. A “yes” vote in parliament, if it comes, won’t immediately make Bougainville independent. But it will set the legal machinery moving. Hard questions such as the future of the island’s contentious Panguna mine remain unresolved, but the vote offers a chance to recognise decades of work from the Bougainvillean and PNG sides that have kept the peace process on track. The legacy of colonialism Bougainville was named by French navigator Louis Antoine de Bougainville in the 18th century, and colonialism has shaped its history ever since. In 1899, it was incorporated into German New Guinea, while the neighbouring Solomon Islands became a British protectorate. Colonial control shifted to Australian occupation in 1914, a move legitimised by the League of Nations in 1920. During the second world war, Japanese forces took over, followed by an American-led invasion in 1943. From 1949, Bougainville was again under Australian control as part of PNG. The dismantling of colonial rule began in 1971, and PNG gained independence in 1975. Bougainville’s decolonisation was left unresolved. The crisis years From 1988 to 1998, Bougainville experienced one of the most severe conflicts in the South Pacific. The Panguna mine was a focal point for grievances related to land ownership, environmental damage, a desire for self-determination and the distribution of mining resources. The mine began operating in 1972 in Central Bougainville, and was once one of the world’s one of the world’s largest copper and gold mines. Owned by a subsidiary of the Australian company Rio Tinto, it was a significant source of revenue for the PNG government. In the late 1980s, the environmental impacts of mining and unequal distribution of its revenues led to violent protests by landowners and the closure of the mine. The PNG government responded with force, and the protests developed into an armed rebellion. Conflict ensued, involving the Bougainville Revolutionary Army, the PNG Defence Force and various local factions. Australia provided indirect military support to PNG forces. A years-long PNG-imposed blockade paralysed Bougainville’s government services and economic activity. An estimated 15,000–20,000 lives were lost in the conflict overall. Attempts to end the fighting began with people from local villages, especially women. They used customary and introduced conflict resolution processes, alongside Christian faith, to lay the groundwork for political negotiations. Eventually, peace talks began in 1998, and an agreement was signed in 2001. Two narratives about how peace was achieved There have long been two narratives about Bougainville’s path to peace. One emphasises regional and international diplomacy, which has involved New Zealand‑facilitated talks in 1997–98, unarmed Australian peace monitoring and UN engagement. The second, backed by many Bougainvillean and PNG leaders, stresses a “light intervention” of international support and notes the distinctly Melanesian approach to peacemaking. This process has been inclusive (involving women’s groups, young people, ex-combatants, faith-based organisations and churches) and patient. The Bougainville Peace Agreement In 2001, the Bougainville Peace Agreement established a framework for Bougainville’s political future. The agreement led to the establishment of the autonomous Bougainville government, a weapons-disposal program, free and fair elections, and a referendum on Bougainville’s future political status. The 2019 referendum gave Bougainvilleans a decisive mandate. Then in August of this year, the autonomous Bougainville government and PNG government – with international support – set out a jointly agreed, phased pathway to translate the referendum result into a constitutional transition. Now, the results must be ratified by PNG’s parliament – the final legislative step in the peace agreement process. A “yes” vote will not itself create independence. It will kick off the legal, administrative and institutional actions needed to move towards self‑government and ultimately independence. A “no” or deferred vote will trigger further consultations and protective measures. Panguna, resources and public understanding Even in PNG, not everyone understands the history of the conflict and the nature of the peace process – especially younger people, including parliamentarians. Some have complained Bougainville’s independence would threaten national unity and set a precedent for other provinces. Complex post-conflict issues remain in Bougainville, including unresolved trauma from the years of conflict. This has exacerbated other forms of violence based on gender and accusations of sorcery. Natural resource governance, especially the future of the still-inactive Panguna mine, also remains uncertain. Local communities have led a process that has just seen Rio Tinto agree to pay US$250 million (A$376 million) to begin addressing the long-term environmental and human cost of the mine. Efforts are also being made to diversify an independent Bougainville’s revenue through fishing, farming and the sustainable approach set out in its “green‑blue economy policy”. For many people, Panguna is both an emblem of past dispossession and a potential source of revenue for an independent Bougainville. For others, its reopening would risk reviving conflict. Across the Pacific, community-led peacebuilding efforts aim to prevent conflict alongside providing environmental resilience. While international security pacts are proliferating, practical security on the ground may depend more on addressing colonial legacies, inequality and the impacts of climate change. A way forward Whatever the outcome of the parliamentary vote, the institutions, relationships and habits of joint work built through the peace process give reason for cautious optimism. The people of Bougainville and Papua New Guinea have done the slow work to get to this point. Those of us watching from outside can take this moment to honour the peace process so far and do what is needed to support its future. Tania Miletic was Project Leader of the Bougainville Senior Leadership Professional Development Program 2023-24, an Australian government program, delivered by the University of Melbourne with financial support from the NZ Government.
da45b84cc5fd1d8d: President Donald Trump is among those who pushed to have Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO. Kevin Dietsch/Getty ImagesThe story may sound familiar: The CEO of one of the largest and most powerful tech companies resigns over sexual misconduct allegations. The move causes the company’s stock to drop by more than 10%, wiping out billions in value. It also raises scrutiny of the company’s board of directors and whether it made the right decisions ahead of the crisis. This could easily describe the turmoil facing Nvidia after the Nov. 12, 2026, ouster of its CEO, Jensen Huang, who remarkably returned to his job just 11 days later. But it actually transpired over 15 years ago at Hewlett Packard, under CEO Mark Hurd. Jensen Huang is just the latest in a long line of CEOs who lost their jobs – albeit in his case temporarily – over personal misconduct. And as with HP, scrutiny is shifting from his behavior to his board – and the decisions that led to his exit. Prominent industry leaders are questioning the board’s original decision to oust him. They include Peter Steinberger of OpenAI, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan – not to mention President Donald Trump, who reportedly directed the effort to get Huang reinstated. As a scholar of management who has researched corporate misconduct, I believe the board had made the right call to force him out. After collecting instances of CEO personal misconduct dating back to 1995, I have repeatedly found that doing nothing, as a board, is worse than doing something. CEO personal misconduct isn’t simply a private matter or an isolated leadership failure. I believe it creates reputational and governance risks for directors and can embolden further misconduct when left unaddressed. It may also signal deeper problems within the organization. But it’s still hard for boards to act, particularly when the CEO is also the company’s founder and a central figure in its success. This is likely why the board chose to reinstate Jensen Huang. And why his return sets a terrible precedent. The costs of misconduct One important change over the years is that boards are becoming more sensitive to misconduct matters due to greater scrutiny by the media and public. They’re also more aware of the consequences for their own job that stem from the board’s performance and entanglement in the misconduct. In fact, directors of companies whose CEOs are involved in personal misconduct exit at a significantly higher rate than normal, either because they choose to leave a messy situation or because they’re forced out due to poor performance, my research shows. One of the better known examples is Best Buy founder Richard Schulze, who stepped down as chairman of the board in 2012 after an internal investigation revealed that he knew about former CEO Brian Dunn’s inappropriate personal relationship with a female employee and failed to report it. Former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker attracted much more negative attention after his second DUI arrest compared to his first. Chip Somodevilla/POOL/AFP via Getty Images Directors are also personally penalized for their association with their company’s corporate misconduct. They may lose their board seats or see other companies they’re associated with take a hit. And if they hold executive positions elsewhere, the misconduct may spill over to damage the reputations of those companies as well. In other words, directors have a rational basis to be concerned about their reputations and how a CEO’s personal misconduct may tarnish it. In the case of Nvidia, questions are now being asked about the rigor of board oversight, the lack of CEO succession planning, and whether the board knew anything about the affairs. These questions have now spread to issues of potential national security risks. Another issue is moral hazard: when someone acts recklessly because they know someone else will bear the cost if things go wrong. Assuming individual directors do face penalties for CEO personal misconduct, they have to address the likelihood of incentivizing further misconduct if the CEO is retained, which would further stain their reputation. My research has found that risk to be high. When CEOs are caught engaging in misconduct and the board doesn’t act, it can create a moral-hazard precedent and emboldens the CEO to behave badly again. In fact, when CEOs engage in repeated personal misconduct, the second instance is often even worse than the first. Take former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker, who was the subject of two publicly reported DUI arrests. The second incident, in 2007, attracted considerably more media attention while prompting criticism of the board for allegedly failing to disclose the first incident in 1991. Christopher Kubasik is another example of a second chance gone wrong. He was recently ousted as CEO of defense contractor L3Harris Technologies, more than 14 years after being forced out of Lockheed Martin following allegations of similar personal misconduct involving an inappropriate relationship. In the case of Nvidia, Jensen reportedly lied to company officials about the nature of his intimate relationships for more than a year. From the board’s perspective, if he lied about this, what else has he lied about? And if they let him off the hook, what would he lie about in the future? In reinstating him, the board said it “was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.” Nvidia’s board has come under more scrutiny for its own oversight after it ousted, then reinstated, its CEO, Jensen Huang. Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images A question of culture Broader, often uncomfortable questions about company culture are also at stake. CEO personal misconduct can be a symptom of a larger cultural problem at the company, my research shows. And it’s often associated with other types of corporate misconduct that affect the very operations of a business. In fact, other types of corporate misconduct frequently occur around a similar time frame as the personal misconduct of an executive. Take Dov Charney’s tenure as CEO of American Apparel. During his leadership, the company faced significant accounting problems in 2009-10 that required it to re-audit several years of financial statements. Around the same time, Charney faced multiple allegations of personal misconduct, including sexual harassment, sexual assault, racist remarks and abusive behavior toward employees. It’s in boards’ interest to grasp that personal misconduct can indicate a larger organizational issue – and, as a result, lead to more scrutiny of the board. With Nvidia, for example, there’s now a spotlight on the company’s organizational culture, its financial dealings and its possible role in skirting U.S. sanctions on Chinese chip import restrictions. The board is likely looking at the totality of the issues and not just the personal misconduct. In the runup to Huang’s return to Nvidia, the public debate had largely been centered on what the company might lose without Jensen Huang at the helm. An equally important question, though, is what the company and its board might risk by retaining a CEO whose conduct has raised serious questions about judgment, trust and organizational oversight. The decision to reinstate him suggests that political pressure can interfere with companies’ hiring and firing for misconduct, and that powerful CEOs are above the normal corporate considerations that would lead to dismissal. The Nvidia case might set a precedent, as other CEOs and boards now know the playbook for getting away with misconduct. It’s a board’s duty to protect its organization from managers who go astray, as legendary investor Warren Buffett noted: “It isn’t fundamental dishonesty that causes people to go in a different direction. It’s human nature. There are plenty of people who are really decent people, intelligent people. … But they just don’t come to grips with reality. And boards usually don’t push them to.” This article was updated on Nov. 23, 2026, to reflect Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO.
