3bb7039d1dd360ac: Chris McGrath/GettyTwo days after the COP31 global climate summit was supposed to finish, the talks in Antalya, Turkey, have come to an end – but not as we might have hoped. Agreement simply could not be reached. The sticking point was the omission of fossil fuels in draft texts. The European Union led a revolt, shattering the consensus needed to adopt the cover text proposed by the Turkish and Australian conveners. In a year of unprecedented climate disasters, a supercharged El Niño and as the world heads inevitably past 1.5 °C of warming, the EU and other nations said that the international process did not meet the moment. Some coverage has suggested the rejection of the cover text is a sign the entire summit was a failure. This isn’t quite right. These texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process. Countries have regularly agreed these political, overarching statements, particularly since the Glasgow meeting in 2021, but they are not a requirement. Its failure does not signal the end of the COP process – or the breakdown of the Paris Agreement. What it may mean is that international climate cooperation will look different from this point onwards. Chris Bowen, the COP31 president of negotiations and Australia’s Minister for Climate Change, speaks to the media after the final session during the second overtime day of the climate talks. Chris McGrath/Getty No mention of the ‘F’ word For many observers, the litmus test for success at COP31 was whether countries could make any headway on the root cause of climate change – fossil fuels. Unfortunately, fossil fuels proved unmentionable. Three years ago at COP28 in Dubai, countries agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels”, marking the first time fossil fuels had explicitly been mentioned in an official decision text in decades of negotiations. The Dubai text was hailed as “the beginning of the end of the fossil fuel era”. But there was little sign that hope would be realised in Turkey. In a repeat of last year’s fraught negotiations at COP30 in Brazil, major fossil fuel producing nations Saudi Arabia and Russia banded together to block any reference in the negotiating outcomes and proposed cover text. Australia and Turkey proposed a compromise – no fossil fuel language in exchange for support for electrification “with the greatest possible use of clean energy”. This seemed to get Saudi Arabia over the line but drew backlash from the European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, and Belize, who rejected the cover text. Brazil took a different approach to the same problem last year. In a bid to break the deadlock, Brazil committed to develop a global strategy to phase out fossil fuels outside the formal negotiating agenda. The roadmap was launched at this year’s summit in Turkey and managed to attract support from big fossil fuel producers such as India, Germany and Nigeria. Countries across the European Union are launching similar roadmaps. Frustration over fossil fuels at COP31 is likely to lead more nations to go outside official talks to progress phase-out efforts. Earlier this year, 57 nations attended the first conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia. Another meeting is planned for next year, co-hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland. Neither the Turkish hosts nor their Australian partners seemed keen to mention fossil fuels. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan was untroubled by the optics of announcing two huge new oilfields in Turkey in his speech at the summit opening. While Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese highlighted the existential risks to Pacific countries from climate change, he made no commitment to stop approving new Australian coal and gas projects. Both leaders much preferred to talk about electrification, namely the flagship “35 by 35” electrification pledge. The goal here is to boost electricity’s share of final energy use globally from around 23% at present to 35% by 2035. Efforts to embed this goal in the cover text failed. But the electrification pledge drew strong support outside official negotiations. More than 75 countries and 180 businesses signed on, including the European Union and China. Activist Greta Thunberg attends a protest at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. Burak Kara/Getty The “COP of action” fails to deliver This year’s climate summit was billed as an “implementation COP”, focused on delivering the pledges countries had already made to address climate change. Overseen by Australia in its role as “president of negotiations”, the formal talks largely focused on the actions countries are taking to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change, whether their response is sufficiently urgent and whether funds aimed at supporting the most vulnerable countries are adequate. It was abundantly obvious that longstanding divisions had not been overcome. Developed countries called for emissions to be cut faster, while developing countries responded by pointing to a lack of financial support to do so. African countries, in particular, stressed that an “implementation COP” was meaningless if rich nations failed to provide the actual resources needed to act. Despite the general gloom, these talks did achieve progress in a few areas. Nations moved forwards on supporting a just transition (shifting to clean energy fairly) via a “phased approach”, as well as improving alignment in climate adaptation, which will help the poorest nations to implement their adaptation plans. But broader efforts to find a way forward on the Paris Agreement’s Global Goal on Adaptation were left unresolved. Decisions stalled in many negotiating rooms in the face of hard “red lines” declared by different blocs of countries. Countries failed to reach any agreement on the vital question of cutting emissions, after Saudia Arabia and Russia blocked a proposed decision. Both are among the world’s top fossil fuel exporting nations. This failure has left the world without any dedicated negotiating process on cutting emissions under the Paris Agreement. It’s possible nations could agree to renew a work program on climate mitigation at next year’s COP32 talks in Ethiopia. What about money for adaptation? Who pays for the costs of climate change has long been a contentious point. Developing countries face the brunt of damage from climate change, but have emitted far less – and have much less money to spend on adaptation. Ahead of COP31, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said talks on new climate finance commitments were “dead in the water”. He urged delegates to focus on implementing existing pledges rather than try for fresh funding. The summit failed to meet even these low expectations. No concrete progress was achieved on the goal of tripling funds for climate adaptation pledged last year at COP30 in Brazil. Ahead of the summit, the Australian government flagged the need to boost global contributions to the official Pacific climate fund. This, too, didn’t eventuate. Rich nations – including Australia – merely re-announced their existing pledges, leaving the Pacific fund A$450 million short of its 2026 target of $749 million. Ironically, the most notable pledge came from the Solomon Islands, a small Pacific nation. Prime Minister Matthew Wale pledged $600,000 to the global Green Climate Fund. “The Pacific did not create this crisis,” he declared. “But we will not stand by and wait for others to act”. A few new commitments arrived by the end of the two week summit from nations such as Canada and Norway. Press and participants watch as a man dressed as a dinosaur performs as part of the Fossil Of The Day award at the COP31 UN climate summit. Burak Kara/Getty Images Defending the science Unusually, climate science was front and centre at COP31. This year, a small bloc of fossil fuel-producing countries has been obstructing the publication of key scientific reports from the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. This year marks the first UN summit since it was officially confirmed the world will overshoot the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C goal by 2030. With the collapse of support for the cover text, statements supporting release of the latest climate science didn’t get approval. All that remained were technical conclusions which “expressed utmost concern” that climate impacts will continue to increase with every increment of global warming. IPCC chair Jim Skea at the opening ceremony of COP31. Previously, he described the stymied outcome of the meeting in Ethiopia as frustrating and disappointing. Chris McGrath/Getty Images Australia on the global stage COP31 gave Australia a unique global role. After being outmanoeuvred in their bid to host the summit, Australia secured a role in overseeing negotiations. Australian Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen and his team had the unenviable task of seeking consensus between 195 countries and the European Union. After the cover text was rejected, Bowen declared Australia had left “nothing on the field” but had faced “unbridgeable red lines.” Hours beforehand, Fijian Climate Minister Lynda Tabuya acknowledged Bowen’s efforts, noting the failure was “not yours to carry […] it is the responsibility of all parties.” Are COP summits still worthwhile? This year’s climate summit took the unenviable record of the longest ever. With consensus seemingly impossible, some civil society representatives dubbed it “the worst COP ever.” Outgoing UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres blamed “powerful fossil fuel interests”, including fossil fuel exporters and corporate lobbyists. Some nations are now calling for urgent reform to negotiations long paralysed by vetoes and disconnected from science. Unfortunately, any change to official voting processes would itself require a consensus decision. Consensus is hard to achieve, but powerful. The power of the Paris Agreement draws on the fact it represents the view of nearly every country – big or small, rich or poor. COP31 President Murat Kurum began the summit expressing hopes this year’s talks would leave a legacy of “working together.” That was a false hope. A more realistic hope is that the collapse of consensus may be the shock the world needs to change course. As former UN climate chief Christiana Figueres has said, we should not see the refusal of more than 130 countries to sign an inadequate deal as a failure. Rather, it might be “a sign of courage”. Jacqueline Peel receives funding from the Australian Research Council. She is affiliated with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, serving as a coordinating lead author in Working Group III (mitigation) for the Seventh Assessment Report. Kathryn Bowen receives funding from Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and Department of Climate Change, Energy, Environment and Water, the World Health Organisation, Wellcome, the Global Fund, Green Climate Fund, Global Environment Facility, Asian Development Bank and World Bank. She is affiliated with the Port Philip EcoCentre and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change where she is a lead author for the Sixth and Seventh Assessment Reports (Working Group II - Impacts, Vulnerability and Adaptation).
d7f1aa6d6e23a0d1: From Hisham Othman

Sadiq Asyraf argues that Pakatan Harapan is blaming the sea for its sinking ship. After Melaka, he says, its leaders pointed to machinery, candidates, turnout, and identity politics while avoiding the deeper problem facing PH.

He is right that PH has a problem. In particular, PKR which contested 10 seats and won none. A party that holds the premiership needs to do better in the Malay and mixed constituencies it is meant to reach.

But PH leaders have also named the larger force shaping those contests. Identity politics has long influenced how Malaysians vote. Many Malay voters remain wary of PH because of DAP’s place in the coalition. When Umno and PAS offer them a common candidate, PH has to compete against both parties’ existing support at once.

PH must examine its machinery and candidates because those are things it can improve. It should also be honest about how much ground it needs to gain. Even an excellent campaign in Melaka would have had to overcome a gap that existed before nominations.
Landslide came from votes BN and PN already had
In 2021, Barisan Nasional and Perikatan Nasional contested against each other in Melaka. BN won 21 seats and PN two. PH won five.
This time, BN and PN backed one candidate in each constituency. Together, they won 24 of the 28 seats. PH retained four and lost one.
The combined BN and PN share of valid votes was 62.7% in 2021 and 63.2% this year. Their share was broadly stable. The change was that the two coalitions now stood on the same side.
Bukit Katil - the seat PH lost - makes the point. Adly Zahari won it in 2021 with 6,805 votes while his BN and PN opponents split 9,463 between them.

This year, Adly received 8,698 votes, but his share fell from 41.6% to 34.5%. With BN’s support, PAS candidate Ridzuan Sarif won 15,305 votes. The electorate had grown, and the combined opposition to Adly was now behind one candidate.
The BN-PN partnership deserves credit for bringing those voters together. Its strength in Melaka also came from support the two sides already had.

That does not mean PH can be complacent. Its statewide share fell from nearly 36% in 2021 to about 29% this year. The changing electorate, a different set of contests and PH’s decision to leave four seats to Bersatu make comparisons imperfect. The decline still deserves scrutiny.
Negeri Sembilan showed a related problem. PH won the largest share of the vote at 40.2%, yet fell from 17 seats to 11 after BN and PN agreed to divide the constituencies between them.

In both states, the way support is distributed matters. PH can win substantial numbers of votes and still struggle to turn them into seats when a larger opposing vote is concentrated behind one candidate.
The bargain moves north
The first hope for PH is that BN and PAS find a national agreement harder to reach than their arrangements in the south.

In Johor, PAS urged supporters to back BN where it had no candidate. In Negeri Sembilan and Melaka, the two sides divided the seats. PAS can now reasonably expect BN to return the favour in the north and on the east coast.

The old PN won 39 of the 40 parliamentary seats across Kedah, Perlis, Kelantan and Terengganu at GE15. Under an incumbency principle, BN would have to stand aside in most of them. That would be difficult for an Umno leadership seeking to reclaim Putrajaya.

Terengganu menteri besar Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar has indicated how PAS sees the negotiations at state level. He has said five seats held by Bersatu representatives could be discussed with BN. PAS holds the other 27 and would expect to defend them.

In Kelantan, BN could press its case for Gua Musang, where it won the Nenggiri state by-election. In Kedah and Perlis, constituencies won by Bersatu under the old PN banner may be contested in negotiations by Umno and Hamzah Zainudin’s Wawasan. Parliamentary and state seats will each have their own local demands.
Then there is the premiership. BN will want enough seats to claim it. PAS has its own ambitions, and Samsuri has rejected the idea that either side should act as a senior partner.

They could agree on seats before the election and decide who leads after the results. They could also fail to reach an agreement and contest separately. The outcome matters greatly to PH, but it will be decided by BN and PN.
A three-way fight is only an opening

At GE15, PH and its allies won 82 parliamentary seats, PN won 74 and BN won 30. Malay voters were divided between the latter two coalitions. After a hung parliament, PH formed a government with BN and parties from Sabah and Sarawak.

A three-way contest at GE16 could again help PH win seats where BN and PN divide the vote. But the conditions facing PH have changed. PKR is under pressure, while DAP has also lost ground in some places. DAP held all four of PH’s seats in Melaka, but its tally in Johor fell from 10 to six, and it failed to win any of the eight seats it contested in Sabah.
The 82 seats won in 2022 are, therefore, a target to defend. They are also 30 short of the 112 needed for a majority.

If PH falls substantially below that figure, even a split between BN and PN may not be enough to keep it in government. The two could contest against each other and still join forces afterwards. If PN emerges as the larger bloc, Samsuri or Hamzah could be among those considered for the premiership. If BN wins more seats, it could seek PN’s support for its own candidate. Parties in Sabah and Sarawak would again have an important say in assembling a majority.
PH’s most immediate task is, therefore, to recover its lost ground, defend as much of its 2022 tally as possible, and seek to remain the largest bloc.
The task facing PKR and DAP
PH has two ways to expand beyond its present support. One is to persuade more Malaysians to vote across established racial and party loyalties.

That happened to an extent in 2018. Anger over the cost of living, GST and 1MDB helped move voters away from BN. Dr Mahathir Mohamad also gave some Malay voters confidence that their interests would carry weight in a government that included DAP. Both helped make PH a viable choice.

A change on that scale by GE16 is possible, but PH cannot count on it. Young voters may bring new priorities, including wages, housing, and the cost of starting a family. Yet GE15 also showed that many young Malay voters were attracted to PN. Research has found that family and community can shape their political choices.

The second route is to add a strong Malay partner. Bersatu played that role in 2018, although it won only 13 parliamentary seats. By GE15, Bersatu and PAS were together in PN, which became the largest bloc drawing primarily on Malay support. PN still ended up outside the federal government.

Khairy Jamaluddin has suggested reviving a partnership along the lines of Barisan Alternatif, which once brought PKR, PAS and DAP together. PAS would bring a substantial Malay base to such an arrangement. But Abdul Hadi Awang has said he would only respond to the prospect of joining Anwar Ibrahim’s government once DAP was out. For now, that makes a reunion a distant prospect.
That leaves PH with work it can begin itself. DAP needs to retain the confidence of its supporters by showing progress on good governance, reforms, and the everyday concerns that brought them to PH.

PKR needs to rebuild its reach in Malay and mixed seats. That requires stronger local machinery, credible candidates chosen early and a clearer account of what the government has delivered. The “sakau” campaign may remind voters of the past, but they also need to hear what PKR intends to do next.

A practical Bumiputera agenda should speak to jobs, skills, business opportunities, and economic security. PKR must show that it can protect Malay interests, lead a multiracial coalition, and hold its ground when it disagrees with DAP. It also needs younger leaders with real responsibilities and a message that speaks to their generation.

There is still time before GE16 for PH to make that case. Whether BN and PAS can agree on northern seats will shape the contest. Whether PH is strong enough to take advantage of a split will depend on what PKR and DAP do with that time.
Hisham Othman is a FMT reader.

b7349dc602250b47: From Anak Negeri

As events unfolded over the past week, and as reported by the media, what was once shrouded in rumour and political theatre has become unmistakably clear – terang lagi bersuluh, like moonlight in a clear sky.
Contrary to public announcements made by those in power, the Negeri Sembilan menteri besar apparently did not submit a resignation letter to the palace.

This clarification emerged at the precise moment when the Yang Dipertuan Besar demonstrated extraordinary magnanimity. Despite the grave constitutional breach committed in September – when the menteri besar and his exco defied royal authority over the illegal proclamation, leading to the revocation of all 10 exco appointments – the Yang Dipertuan Besar granted an audience to the menteri besar as he sought to retract the earlier position, pledge allegiance anew and make amends.
Caught in a larger game?

For months, many ordinary Anak Negeri wondered how someone who hails from Juasseh in Kuala Pilah – a heartland steeped in adat perpatih and expected loyalty to Seri Menanti – could ever have stood at the forefront of a challenge against the Yang Dipertuan Besar.

Media accounts surrounding the disputed resignation letter offered a sobering explanation. Far from acting as an independent architect of treason, the menteri besar appears to have functioned largely as a figurehead, constrained by instructions and pressure exerted by more powerful figures outside the state.

When someone's political survival depends on party directives from afar rather than the mandate of his own people, even the highest office in the state administration risks being reduced to an instrument of someone else’s design.
Progress stalled by coalition horse-trading

When the Yang Dipertuan Besar extended royal grace and the menteri besar moved to retract the September letter to the Conference of Rulers, the people of Negeri Sembilan dared to hope that this damaging chapter was finally coming to a close.

After weeks of governance without a functioning exco, ordinary citizens wanted the conversation to return to bread-and-butter priorities: attracting quality investment into Nilai and Senawang, strengthening local infrastructure and preparing a sound 2027 state budget.
Instead, the path forward has once again been obstructed by internal power struggles in a political entity.
It was this particular political entity that elevated what began as a clan-based deposed chieftain's refusal to come to terms with his dismissal into a full-blown national crisis.

It is a bitter irony that a political entity which routinely proclaims itself the foremost defender of the Malay rulers and the dignity of the Malays has allowed factional manoeuvring to take precedence over stability in Negeri Sembilan.

With the state legislative assembly supposedly scheduled to convene on Nov 26 and the 2027 budget due to be tabled on Nov 27, the swearing-in of a new exco reportedly stalled over last-minute withdrawals and disputes over who gets to occupy the proposed seats.

To us Anak Negeri, the message is unmistakable: the 2027 state budget and the livelihoods of ordinary citizens of Negeri Sembilan have been pushed to the back seat while politicians haggle over the menteri besar's chair and exco privileges. In that calculation, the rakyat of Negeri Sembilan barely register, and genuine deference to the Yang Dipertuan Besar appears secondary to factional leverage.

Yet one must also ask: why do these assemblymen – whom we, the voters of Negeri Sembilan, elected – defer so obediently to their political masters, when it was the electorate who empowered those very masters in the first place? Are we Anak Negeri only relevant at the ballot box, only for our interests to be cast aside once the election is over? Do our elected assemblymen not even have the courage to stand up to their political masters in the interest of us, the people of Negeri Sembilan?
Customary defiance and the rule of law

At the same time, illegal defiance on the customary front stubbornly persists. Despite the October gazette formalising the removal and replacement of deposed chieftains, one chieftain and all the former chieftains continue to illegally defy the decrees of the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang.

Their legal position, however, has already been stripped of any illusion of sovereign immunity. The Court of Appeal has made clear that they do not stand above the law. In fact, in the eyes of the courts, they are subject to the same legal accountability as any ordinary Anak Negeri.

With committal proceedings already scheduled in the Seremban High Court – including the hearing set for Dec 15 – and leave granted for further contempt actions, the judicial process is steadily closing the space for defiance. The only difference is that while ordinary citizens face the law alone, these figures continue to operate as though shielded by external political patronage.
A call to constitutional order

Whatever political compromises might be reached in the coming days, the people of Negeri Sembilan should remember this episode clearly. We have seen first-hand how external political interests can override both the constitutional dignity of the state and the welfare of fellow Anak Negeri.

In order to restore lasting peace to Negeri Sembilan, wisdom within Luak Johol is urgently needed. May the Biduanda clan members (Anak Waris) in Johol look past political inducements, uphold the true spirit of adat perpatih and take decisive customary action to set their clan in order once and for all.

May the federal authorities enforce the law consistently and without hesitation against online instigators who continue to spread seditious hatred and falsehoods against the royal institution of Negeri Sembilan.

Negeri Sembilan belongs to all its people, not only to any single clan, and rests upon the constitutional wisdom of its Malay ruler. No political entity – and no external power broker – has the right to hold the state’s future hostage.

b13524eb59bc2d9c: From Sadiq Asyraf

Within 24 hours of losing Melaka, Pakatan Harapan (PH) offered several reasons for its defeat. The coalition's communications director, Fahmi Fadzil, pointed to candidates' preparedness, the youth vote, turnout and weak rural machinery.
Amanah vice-president Dzulkefly Ahmad blamed politics of hostility and hatred by Barisan Nasional (BN) and Perikatan Nasional (PN).
Melaka DAP chairman Khoo Poay Tiong blamed identity politics, while PH election director Amirudin Shari said support was intact and the coalition needed a new political realignment.

PH chairman Anwar Ibrahim's only public word after the results was a social media post congratulating BN and declaring that "it is now time for us to move forward by prioritising the people's interests".

It offered no explanation for the defeat. His lieutenants supplied that. Where their explanations look inward at all, they stop at candidates and machinery; the rest place the cause outside PH. None names the party that contested 10 seats and won nothing, which happens to be the prime minister's own.
A diagnosis that points elsewhere

Framing theory explains why this matters. How a defeat is explained shapes what gets fixed afterwards. A defeat blamed on opponents, candidates and machinery calls for better messaging, better allies and better logistics. A defeat blamed on what PH's parties offer voters calls for something harder.
PH's post-mortem so far acknowledges operational weaknesses but stops short of PKR's deeper electoral problem. Call it a shallow post-mortem.

PH's campaign branded its opponents "sakau", yet the "corporate mafia" allegations first reported by Bloomberg in February have hung over its own government, and the royal commission of inquiry sought by DAP has yet to be formed. A charge of plunder carries little weight when voters can see similar questions closer to home.
For PKR supporters, Bersama made a convenient scapegoat. It is led by former PKR deputy president Rafizi Ramli, and after Johor, even DAP's Tony Pua called it a spoiler that cost PH seats.

Yet even under the unrealistic assumption that every Bersama vote would have gone to PH, the coalition still lost all 10 seats where both stood and BN or PN won. The closest is Machap Jaya, where BN polled 6,686 votes against 4,731 for PH and Bersama combined. Bersama competed for the urban vote but decided no seat.
Amirudin's own evidence fares no better. As proof that support had held, he pointed to Bukit Katil, where Adly Zahari's vote rose from 6,805 in 2021 to 8,698 this year.

The 2021 Melaka election preceded automatic voter registration and the lower voting age of 18, so this was the state's first poll under the expanded roll. Bukit Katil's electorate grew by 39%, from 25,410 to 35,359. Adly's share fell from 41.6% to 34.5%.
A rising raw vote in an electorate that has grown by two-fifths is no proof of resilience. Offering it as one is the shallow post-mortem in miniature.
A head without legs
Across its 10 seats, PKR took 24.3% of the vote – the lowest of PH's three components. Amanah managed 26.3% in its seven seats and DAP 50.4% in its seven.

The sharpest results came where the Prime Minister's Office was on the ballot. His political secretary, Azman Abidin, took 37.4% in Paya Rumput, while Farzana Hayani Nasir, an officer in his office, took 27.9% in Kelebang. During the campaign, Anwar urged voters to choose representatives with a "direct line" to his office. Voters in both seats declined the offer.

In Melaka, BN worked as a coalition because its lead party also carried its vote. PH worked the other way round: PKR holds the premiership, while DAP won all four of PH's seats and supplied more than half of its total vote.

PKR was meant to be the multiracial bridge to the Malay and mixed seats that DAP cannot reach. State polls are not a general election, and PKR may yet hold the urban seats it won in 2022. In these four contests, though, it has ridden as a passenger.
The realignment already tried

Amirudin's call for realignment extends the shallow post-mortem, looking for new partners to cover a gap in the coalition. Bersatu, long criticised by PH supporters over the Sheraton Move, faced no PH candidate in Lendu, Sungai Udang, Pantai Kundor and Bemban, and Amirudin told PH members to respect the decision to cede Bemban. The two still clashed in Kelebang, Pengkalan Batu and Ayer Keroh.

Whatever the arrangement, it delivered little. Bersatu won none of its seven seats, lost five deposits and polled 3.2% statewide, less than Bersama. In Bemban, it finished third with 11.5%, behind the Bersama candidate whom PH supporters had spent the campaign deriding.

Melaka fits a larger pattern. Across the four state elections since Sabah last November, PKR has won four of the 58 seats it contested: one in Sabah, one in Johor, two in Negeri Sembilan and none in Melaka. A party that wins under 7% of the seats it contests no longer worries its opponents or reassures its partners.

If the review by PH's presidential council settles on Bersama and racial campaigning, it will be accurate in parts and wrong in its conclusion. The sea did not sink this ship. The prime minister's party is struggling to win the Malay and mixed seats it exists to contest, and its leaders would rather talk about something else.
Sadiq Asyraf is a political communication and media warfare analyst.

29b102c06477d96e: Constitutional jurists from time immemorial have recognised a commonsense truth: judgments are not pronounced by persons possessing the stature of prophets or saints of the rule of law.
Judges are human institutions, fallible by design, operating within adversarial constraints and on the evidence presented before them.
It is for this precise reason that, in almost all Commonwealth jurisdictions, the constitution preserves the right of the constitutional head of state to exercise the prerogative of mercy.

In most countries, that prerogative is exercised on a relatively low threshold of justification, not to defeat justice, but to temper it with mercy and to correct latent miscarriages arising from the inherent limitations of the judicial process.

Our king, by decreeing that Najib pay his RM50 million fine and serve the remainder of his sentence as a prisoner under house arrest, has issued one of the most brilliant and balanced decrees I have witnessed in my judicial career.
The decree is constitutionally sound, beneficial to the nation, protective of institutional dignity, and conducive to the advancement of social justice.

It also demonstrates that the Malay rulers will not descend into gutter politics, nor be swayed by low-level adversarial advocacy, social media agitation, or institutional gatekeepers who seek to weaponise the prerogative of mercy for partisan ends.

In my considered view, the SRC and 1MDB cases against Najib, conducted without the presence of Jho Low and other principal actors, alleged accomplices, aiders and abettors, who have neither been charged nor jointly charged, rest on an incomplete factual substratum that is not fit for conclusive judicial determination.
The prosecution's edifice rests substantially on the conduct of an absent principal architect.

To attempt to prove dishonest intent and knowledge through secondary and relayed evidence while the alleged principal orchestrator remains at large and unexamined renders the case constitutionally incomplete for a definitive finding beyond reasonable doubt.
Najib was appointed prime minister by a previous Yang di-Pertuan Agong pursuant to Articles 40 and 43 of the Federal Constitution.

Given the obvious evidentiary incompleteness surrounding the charges, it was incumbent upon the apex court, in the exercise of its constitutional judicial power, to consider the broader constitutional equilibrium.

Under oath jurisprudence, the apex court possesses inherent constitutional jurisdiction to issue suo motu orders and directions in the interests of justice, the preservation of the constitution, and the prevention of constitutional anomalies.

This, to my mind, would include directing that a matter be placed before the Malay rulers for appropriate action and decree, and, where necessary, directing the government to facilitate such a decree through appropriate constitutional amendments and legislative provisions.

Such an approach would be preferable to permitting the government and its agencies to invite the courts into an exercise akin to searching for hair in an eggshell, a task that risks straining judicial jurisdiction beyond its constitutional limits while simultaneously creating disharmony among citizens.
The prerogative of pardon is a constitutional exception to the principle of finality in judicial decisions.

It is not unusual throughout the Commonwealth for judicial decisions to be perceived as being affected by constitutional, political, prosecutorial, racial, religious, conflict of interest or jurisprudential bias, among other considerations.
In such circumstances, the ultimate constitutional remedy available to a convicted person is the prerogative of mercy.
It therefore behoves the public to be guided by the Malay rulers, who remain the supreme guardians of both the constitution and the rule of law.

8c3ea6e5a4b44538: From Moaz Nair
Action beats reaction. Just days ago, in the early hours of Nov 18, a police operation tracked down an armed serial robber to a hotel in Chow Kit.

The man, suspected of posing as a taxi driver to prey on women and senior citizens in at least 24 robberies, opened fire the moment officers raided his room, forcing police to return fire and neutralise the threat.
Barely a week earlier in Kepong, a 26-year-old police lance corporal had his hand severed in an attack by a dual-machete-wielding assailant who was subsequently shot dead.

These incidents lay bare the lethal reality on Malaysia's streets today. Yet, whenever such shootouts occur, a familiar debate resurfaces among policymakers, legal scholars and human rights advocates over how law enforcement should confront violent criminals.

On one side are those who insist on a strictly defensive, peacekeeping posture. On the other are those who recognise that against hardened, heavily armed syndicates, a proactive, offensive strategy is essential to protect innocent lives.

While critics frequently warn against shifting away from a traditional defensive model, forcing police officers into a purely reactive stance puts both the public and the officers themselves at a severe, potentially fatal disadvantage.
The tactical reality

In law enforcement, there is a fundamental tactical truth: action is faster than reaction. Waiting for an armed suspect to draw a firearm or swing a machete can cost the lives of officers and innocent bystanders alike.

When intelligence confirms a severe, imminent threat – such as a serial robber holed up with a loaded weapon in the heart of Kuala Lumpur – pre-emptive neutralisation is not a reckless choice. It is a tactical necessity.

Furthermore, a strictly defensive posture overlooks a critical moral and legal question: what about the constitutional right to life of the police officers themselves? Unlike ordinary citizens who can retreat from danger, frontline officers are sworn to run towards it.

Denying them the authority to take decisive, offensive action against lethal threats – or subjecting every split-second survival decision to second-guessing – risks demoralising the very force tasked with keeping society safe.
A hesitant police force is an ineffective police force, and criminals are the first to exploit that hesitation.
Deterrence and disruption

Criminological evidence and deterrence theory reinforce the value of targeted, proactive enforcement. Research on "focused deterrence" and intelligence-led operations consistently shows that concentrating decisive police power on high-risk offenders and violent crime hotspots yields significant reductions in firearm violence and robberies.

When hardened criminals know that law enforcement will respond with overwhelming, decisive force, the perceived cost of carrying or using illegal weapons rises dramatically, discouraging violent crime before it occurs.

Offensive policing is equally vital for dismantling organised crime. Specialised task forces executing pre-dawn or night raids on armed syndicates disrupt plots before they unfold – preventing kidnappings, armed robberies and targeted killings before innocent citizens are ever placed in the line of fire.
Accountability within the rule of law

Legal scholars and community advocates rightly caution that in a civil society, the role of the police is to apprehend suspects for trial, not to act as judge and executioner. An unchecked "shoot-first" mentality would indeed erode due process and public trust.
However, adopting a proactive, offensive strategy against armed threats does not mean abandoning the rule of law.

Under Malaysian legal frameworks – such as Section 100 of the Penal Code governing the right of private defence and the inspector-general’s Standing Orders – even elite tactical units conducting preemptive raids remain strictly bound by the principles of necessity and proportionality.
Lethal force is only legally justified to prevent death or grievous hurt.
Protecting the right to life
A civil society survives because it delegates the legitimate use of force to the state to maintain order and protect the innocent.

Supporting a proactive, intelligence-led offensive against armed criminals does not undermine human rights; rather, it upholds the most fundamental human right of all: the right of law-abiding citizens and police officers to live free from violent terror.
When confronting those who wield deadly weapons, the state cannot afford to merely react. It must act decisively to protect life.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

402e4abf38c942a1: In South Asia, survivors of sexual and physical abuse are often met with judgment and stigma
Originally published on Global Voices
Photo via Pratistha Gautam. Used with permission.
Editorial note: This article contains mention of gender-based violence, sexual assault, violence against children, and child sexual abuse, which may be triggering for some readers.

November 25 to December 10, 2026, marks the UN’s 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence. However, even as gender-based violence gets more recognition globally, survivors are still struggling to access social or legal justice. South Asia is no exception to this. Global Voices sat down with one survivor of childhood abuse who uses her experience to fuel her advocacy work today.

South Asia is home to nearly one quarter of the world’s population, woven with a diverse, culture-driven fabric where women are often celebrated as goddesses. However, this veneration doesn’t necessarily mean South Asian women are safe or free from abuse.

In Nepal, there are far too many examples of crimes against women and girls. For instance, Nirmala Panta, 13, was found dead in a sugarcane field — a case which has remained unsolved since 2018. Bhagirathi Bhatta, 17, was choked to death when returning home from school in 2021, and Inisha BK, 16, was found unconscious in the Janagaran Community Forest in Surkhet in early 2026. A similar yet shocking case is that of a 3-year-old Garima, who was found dead inside an abandoned house in Jeetpur in southern Nepal. While these tragic rape and murder cases leave deep scars in Nepal’s national psyche, even more cases go unheard and unreported.

Sparking a nationwide outrage, such cases force the country to confront a collective shame. They raise questions around human morality, diminishing trust and affection in society, and breakdowns in the legal justice system. In the face of these atrocities, women took to the streets, demanding justice and accountability. But their calls fell on deaf ears.
Pratistha Gautam’s story

“I was 11 years old when I was sexually abused by my close maternal uncle for four days,” said Pratishtha Gautam in an online interview with Global Voices in November 2026. Opening up about this incident was a real challenge for her, yet she was committed to sharing her story.

Her childhood was by no means easy. She moved regularly as a child, and at six years old, she was sent to her grandparent’s house for a year because her parents had to move away to address their employment needs. This separation made her feel neglected and she felt that her parents loved her younger brother more. This contributed to a sense of emotional distance and detachment from her family.

Later, at the age of 11, she was left in the care of her mother’s cousin while her younger brother was hospitalized and receiving medical treatment. It was during this time that she experienced sexual abuse at the hands of someone she had known and trusted as a family member, who took away her innocence.

After four days of abuse, she escaped when the abuser fled after she began calling out for help. Finally getting a chance to flee from danger, she “rushed to my room, quickly happened to lock the door by chance, thankfully, and began to scream out to my neighbors.” She had witnessed men mistreating women growing up and feels lucky that her cries weren’t met with indifference.
The abuse only compounded her challenges. As she says, “It was not easy at all.”

The experience has left her with scars: “I have been awakened with nightmares since that incident, making my sleep extremely difficult.” She also suffers from panic attacks when she sees material about sexual abuse. She describes feeling like her heart is swollen and being torn apart. When triggered, she often freezes up and dissociates.

According to research from the American Academy of Pediatrics journal, child sexual abuse can be incredibly detrimental to a person’s long-term mental well-being. Child abuse survivors are more likely to suffer from anxiety disorders, depression, eating disorders and disturbances, sleep disruption and insomnia, and dissociation, as well as adverse physical health conditions and attachment issues, according to the Center of Expertise on Child Sexual Abuse.

This highlights the immense scale of pain that many children experience when they are victims of sexual abuse. Not everyone is able to speak out about such abuses. This is particularly true in South Asia, where there is a social stigma around abuse, due to entrenched ideas around “purity.”

She resents suggestions that it is women’s responsibility to not “tempt” men or draw attention to themselves. “Why should we be the ones to cover ourselves up?” she asks. She refuses to hide and stay silent while her abuser “is living free somewhere.” She refuses to remain invisible.

Even as many countries make strides in gender equality, gender-based violence continues to be a major issue. In a 2023 report, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that nearly one in three (31.6 percent) of women worldwide have been subjected to either physical and/or sexual violence in their lifetime — roughly 840 million women and girls.

At the root of gender-based violence lies a belief in male superiority. Not all men would openly endorse this belief, yet many see themselves as protectors of the women in their lives: their sisters, mothers, girlfriends, and wives. But this notion of protection is deeply flawed, especially when it comes at the cost of women’s freedom, mobility, access to opportunities, dreams, and agency.

Gautam recognizes this notion in her own upbringing. She had dreams of her own and was ready to chase them, but the universe had a different plan for her. She kept her independence through consistent stubbornness and determination.
A trauma that persists

Today, Gautam lives in Adelaide in South Australia. She suffers from complex PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder) and works as a mental health clinician helping other survivors of abuse. She reflected, in a heavy tone, on being a thousand miles away from home but safe and independent.
Gautam feeding a child. Image via Pratistha Gautam. Used with permission.

PTSD and insomnia aren’t the only consequences of her abuse. While she was once married, she struggled to cope with her trauma, and it negatively impacted her relationship, eventually leading to divorce.

As part of her treatment, Gautam has met regularly with psychotherapists over the years. Eventually, even that wasn’t enough. She put everything on hold for a year and gave herself time and space to focus on her mental health. She believes she would have difficulty living a normal life and still struggles with relationships. “I hate men. I used to hate them and still have trust issues,” she said.

Even as she struggles to process her own trauma, she also works to help others recover from abuse and offers pro bono psychological counseling. Being part of the solution has in some ways helped her heal. Her passion as a mental health clinician goes beyond her own individual experiences to the collective — a reminder to be empathetic as humans first.

While she primarily works in Australia, she is also committed to helping women back in her home country of Nepal. She has collaborated with Rakshya Nepal, an organization in Nepal that protects women and girls from sexual exploitation and trafficking.
Reflecting back on the choices she made, she said, “I cannot imagine if I could afford this luxury of mental space if I were not in Australia.”

This is also a testament to how South Asia treats survivors of sexual and physical abuse — even if they gather the courage to speak the truth, too often they are met with judgment and scorn. Part of this is due to limited regard for mental health, but it’s also about entrenched gender roles and strong societal expectations. There is a popular saying in Nepal reflecting these persistent gender dynamics: “timi ta chori manche ho ni” and “chora manche ho ni,” which roughly translates to “you are a girl, and boys will be boys.”
Written by Susmita Aryal
6f2d9f153e249ab8: Following the 2026 state elections, many are predicting that Umno and Perikatan Nasional (PN) will team up and win power in the next general election (GE).

Most analysts see it as an almost certain clash between PH and a PAS-led PN in the peninsula. Some argue that GE16 will be fought primarily on traditional flashpoints: Malay rights, Islamic values, economic delivery, and non-Malay frustrations.
That may be true, but I think this election is more likely to boil down to a dramatic contest of political agility and manoeuvres between Ahmad Zahid Hamidi and Anwar Ibrahim.

While East Malaysia’s blocs in Sabah and Sarawak will—as always—play a decisive kingmaker role post-election to protect local autonomy, the battle to capture Putrajaya itself remains a peninsula-driven contest. Within that crucible, GE16 will essentially be a battle of wills and operational skill between two men who know how to survive at the top.

Zahid's core competency is political engineering. He treats relationships as leverage, public statements as bargaining signals, and possesses a feel for power dynamics that is probably unmatched in modern Malaysian politics.

Yet, while his "blue wave" narrative resonates powerfully with Malay voters, it does not travel cleanly to the urban, mixed, and non-Malay constituencies that ultimately decide a national majority—though Umno relies on its traditional Barisan Nasional coalition mechanisms to manage multi-ethnic seats.

Conversely, Anwar’s strength lies in policy, narrative, and survival. A reformist with international credibility and a coherent platform, Anwar has ridden the waves of triumph and defeat, navigated various crises, and risen to become prime minister.
He is waging a war of attrition, using his control over the national budget and administrative levers to delay the electoral clock while Zahid tries to force an early hand.
To understand why this duel will define GE16, we must look back at how their paths have intertwined over the last three decades.

When the bitter fallout between then-Umno president Mahathir Mohamad and his deputy Anwar erupted in the late 1990s, Zahid—serving as Umno Youth chief—initially backed Anwar. Yet, after Anwar’s sacking in 1998, Zahid quickly pivoted, reconciled with Mahathir, and demonstrated the classic Umno survival instinct: prioritising pragmatism over loyalty.

From that point, Zahid embarked on a meticulously calculated ascent: consolidating his base in Perak, building a formidable personal network, becoming Umno’s deputy president, and finally taking the top spot in 2018.

Following the 2022 humiliation when Umno won just 26 seats, calls for his resignation mounted. He weathered the storm, teamed up with Anwar to secure the post of deputy prime minister, and used his proximity to power to reassert Umno’s relevance.

Anwar, for his part, pursued his long game: forming PKR, driving the Reformasi movement, riding the 2008 opposition surge, and eventually making an uneasy truce with his arch-rival Mahathir to wrest power in 2018. But political betrayals caused Mahathir’s government to collapse, paving the way for short-lived administrations under Muhyiddin Yassin and Ismail Sabri Yaakob.

The inconclusive 2022 general election threw Anwar and Zahid together into an improbable partnership. Zahid secured ministerial perks and shared authority, and by December 2025, the Attorney General’s Chambers granted him a discharge not amounting to an acquittal (DNAA) on the 47 corruption charges involving the Yayasan Akalbudi fund.
Critics blasted the move as a classic manoeuvre to shield allies and buy loyalty, though it has consistently been denied.
Since then, Zahid has supercharged Umno's stature among Malay supporters by leaning into the reliable narrative of Malay unity and perceived threats to Malay dominance.

The resulting PAS-Umno tactical cooperation benefits both parties. This momentum was reflected in the 2026 state elections, though formulas varied: in Johor, BN swept 48 of 56 seats alone (while PN supporters were quietly instructed to back BN in uncontested seats), whereas in Negeri Sembilan and Melaka, BN and PN formally shared seats.
True to form, Zahid is keeping all options open by refusing to commit to a formal GE16 pact with PN, executing a masterstroke that forces both PH and PN to compete for Umno's favour.

Simultaneously, he has tightened his internal grip: the Umno Supreme Council has postponed party polls to a date no later than six months after GE16, and an "unconditional open-door" policy has welcomed back former rivals like Khairy Jamaluddin and Hishammuddin Hussein. Zahid is building a broad electoral coalition while keeping his own leadership uncontested.

Demonstrating his pragmatic ambition further, Zahid acknowledged Gabungan Parti Sarawak's (GPS) absolute regional dominance by confirming that BN would sit out the Sarawak state election to respect East Malaysian autonomy and keep the federal focus razor-sharp on the peninsula.

Conversely, Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan has been battling severe internal friction. PKR has suffered heavy blows: high-profile figures like Rafizi Ramli and Nik Nazmi Nik Ahmad departed to form Parti Bersama Malaysia, Nurul Izzah went on indefinite leave as deputy president, and the party suffered a major rout in Melaka.

Anwar's prospects now hinge heavily on timing. PH’s parliamentary term runs until December 2027, with GE16 legally due by February 2028. Every month of delay buys both sides different advantages: Zahid consolidates his machine, while Anwar attempts to deliver tangible economic relief.
If Anwar can produce visible improvements in the cost of living by late 2027 and push through more reforms, the votes will return.

Furthermore, PH retains a structural edge in the urban and mixed constituencies that decide a national majority. State elections are typically less diverse and more heavily Malay-majority, making the "blue wave" less effective on a national scale.

Moreover, non-Malay support for PH is driven less by uncritical loyalty and more by a structural fear of the alternative (a PAS-led PN). As the Malay vote consolidates behind BN-PN, non-Malay voters increasingly rally behind DAP and PH as a defensive counterweight, keeping PH viable nationally even as it bleeds support in heartland seats.
Also, as seat negotiations between Umno and PAS heat up, deep fractures in the Malay-Muslim vote will be exposed.

Yet, as these electoral calculations play out, Zahid carries a heavy legal overhang. The Court of Appeal allowed the Malaysian Bar's judicial review challenge in May 2026, the Federal Court granted Zahid and the AG leave to appeal in October 2026, and the High Court has slated case management for June 2027, with the full hearing deferred until the Federal Court appeal concludes. It is a sword of Damocles that is certain to become a major campaign issue.

Ultimately, GE16 will be a contest of political operators. The 2026 state elections suggest Zahid holds the momentum. However, Anwar’s control over the electoral timeline, his economic levers, and the structural divide between state and national electorates keep the race wide open.

What began as a clash between reform and patronage has evolved into a masterclass in machine politics versus institutional statecraft. The next general election will not be decided by slogans or promises alone—it will be decided by who plays the sharper game over the next six to twelve months.

52e6204978a8560b: The Najib Razak saga has, in many ways, eclipsed even Anwar Ibrahim’s ‘Reformasi’ struggles, which saw many of us old-timers go through some very harrowing times.
Both were deputy prime ministers and served under Dr Mahathir Mohamad.
Their parallels are striking. Anwar was sacked, charged, convicted and spent time in prison before being pardoned, later rising to become prime minister.
Najib took the opposite route. An Umno prime minister, no less, he lost power, was charged, convicted and served time, before being pardoned twice, albeit conditionally.

Despite the unbridled demonisation of the DAP and non-Malays as traitors out to wreck a nation, it must be stressed that it was a courageous Malay judge—a woman no less—who sent the former Umno president to jail.
Now, there are many “firsts” in this saga.

Najib went on trial in what became known as “the world’s largest kleptocracy case”, a notorious distinction that brought his party and the country the sort of international headlines it could have done without.
Secondly, Najib is the first prime minister to be incarcerated in Malaysia.
And thirdly, this is the first documented house arrest case in the country, even preceding a proposed new law that the government intends to introduce in Parliament.
Now there are many views about the former Pekan MP’s house arrest.
Among them is the perceived double-standard. Why is Najib allowed these perks, while other convicts are not?
There is also the matter of the king’s decision in Najib’s pardon application. Must the king adhere to the pardon board’s advice? And should the minutes have been declassified?
As for the king’s decision to allow Najib to be placed under house arrest, that is his prerogative, one that is enshrined in our Federal Constitution.
He has chosen to exercise it in Najib’s favour for reasons known only to him. Not being privy to that decision, and without any insights into his reasons, it would not be proper to comment on it.
But it has to be emphasised that there is no prefect constitution, no perfect rendition of history, and no perfect interpretation of religion.
Hence, we need to rely on the wisdom and experience of those who make such decisions with the nation’s best interests at heart.
The recent publication of the minutes of that meeting of the pardons board has given the public a rare insight into what transpired and the stance taken by each board member.
That said, the published document should not trigger a blame game.
Whatever one feels about the decision, it must be acknowledged that it went through due process.
If Malaysians believe that process should be improved or changed, the proper avenue is through their elected representatives in the Dewan Rakyat.
For my part, I am satisfied that due process has been observed and therefore respect and accept the decision reached.

Still, I find it comical that Umno has been so worked up over the declassification of the document simply because it was not accompanied by a royal decree, even arguing that the omission was somehow tantamount to disrespecting the Malay rulers.
Has that same respect been shown to Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir amid the seemingly unending constitutional crisis in Negeri Sembilan, a controversy that bears Umno's fingerprints all over it?
The time has come for us to put the brouhaha over Najib's house arrest to rest.
At the end of the day, Najib was convicted for a crime, served some time in jail, applied for a pardon, as allowed by law, and was granted one.
Placing him under house arrest does not erase his criminal conviction.
There is no value in bickering over the merits of the house arrest as it serves no purpose other than to instigate one party and weaponise the issue.
It is time we focused on the more important stuff, like the bread-and-butter issues affecting ordinary Malaysians. That is a far more worthy cause.

9b6b75dea9243402: Tony Pua has apparently discovered a remarkable constitutional innovation: when the king grants clemency against objections, publish the objections and call it accountability. Yet the awkward question remains. Does displaying dissent explain the constitutional decision, or merely provide political cover for those embarrassed by its outcome?
On Nov 18, Pua circulated pages described as declassified minutes from the Sept 18 Federal Territories Pardons Board meeting concerning former prime minister Najib Razak.

According to news reports, Attorney-General Dusuki Mokhtar and federal territories minister Hannah Yeoh opposed house arrest. The king nevertheless approved a conditional pardon. These reported extracts warrant authentication and contextual examination; a Facebook upload is not itself a constitutional certificate.
Let us distinguish three matters politicians seem determined to blend: the right to disagree during deliberations, the authority to decide, and the legality of disclosing deliberations afterwards.

Article 42 establishes the constitutional pardoning framework. Recording objections does not confer a veto. Nor does royal authority automatically exempt officials from explaining how records were classified, accessed and released.

Pua’s intervention invites sharper scrutiny precisely because he presents disclosure as vindication. Vindication of what? That DAP representatives objected? The minutes reportedly establish that much. That the government’s political conscience is therefore spotless? That is a considerably longer leap, requiring evidence rather than screenshots and self-congratulation.

DAP cannot simultaneously celebrate constitutional procedure when it documents ministerial dissent and treat the resulting royal decision as someone else’s political inconvenience. A constitutional monarchy is not a buffet where parties select the minutes they enjoy and leave the decision behind. If dissent was properly recorded, publicly explain it. If the decision was lawful, respect it. Neither proposition requires surrendering criticism of corruption.

Umno is justified in demanding a clear account of the disclosure process. Its leaders have asked whether the documents were officially declassified, who authorised circulation, and whether the palace was consulted. Those are legitimate institutional questions, although assertions that publication necessarily constitutes an insult to the king require a specific legal and factual foundation. Defending royal dignity should strengthen constitutional precision, not replace it with outrage.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim faces the more uncomfortable examination. He has publicly defended every prisoner’s access to the pardon process and acknowledged the king’s constitutional role. Fine words. But was his administration’s handling of disclosure governed by a consistent rule, or by whichever political controversy happened to be burning that week? The public deserves an answer from Putrajaya, not another seminar on principles everyone claims to cherish.

The comparison with Anwar’s 2018 pardon is unavoidable. Wan Saiful Wan Jan has called for those Pardons Board minutes to be released, too. That demand does not prove irregularity in either pardon. It does expose the weakness of selective transparency. If publication serves public confidence today, what principled distinction governs disclosure of earlier proceedings? Privacy, privilege and national security may justify redactions; political convenience is not a constitutional doctrine.

There is an important qualification. Minutes capture deliberation, not necessarily every legal consideration or the full operative instrument. Readers should resist pretending five circulated pages settle all constitutional questions. Officials must establish authenticity, classification status, completeness, and applicable disclosure authority before political protagonists announce their preferred verdict.

My assessment is that this affair tests the government’s credibility more severely than Najib’s political fortunes. A government preaching institutional reform must demonstrate procedures that survive partisan advantage. Publish a reasoned disclosure policy, identify the competent authorising authority, and apply equivalent standards to comparable pardons. Where confidentiality is required, explain its legal basis without exposing protected deliberations.

And Pua? He is entitled to criticise Najib, challenge clemency and defend his former colleagues. He is not entitled to confuse proof of opposition with proof of governmental consistency. The former may fit neatly into a social media post; the latter demands accountability across administrations, personalities, and inconvenient precedents.
The king does not require politicians to manufacture unanimity. The Constitution requires institutions to understand their responsibilities.
Umno should defend that distinction firmly; DAP and PH should answer it without theatrical evasion; Anwar should insist upon rules rather than improvisation.
When constitutional records become partisan ammunition, the real scandal is not disagreement. It is a government unable to explain who loaded the weapon, under what authority, and why only now.
Azam Mohd is an FMT reader.

8f13969a68ed3f91: Having agreed to new peace talks with Ukrainian and American representatives earlier this month, Russian negotiators suddenly wanted to discuss the European security order, too.
It was an obvious attempt to divert attention from the urgent need, after almost five years, for a ceasefire in Russian president Vladimir Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine.
While the inept US negotiating duo of Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff seemed to go along with the Russian proposal, the Europeans saw right through it.
They pointed out that there is already an agreed European security order, to which Russia is a signatory. The only problem is that Russia is blatantly violating it. That is what must be discussed.

The European security order is basically no different from what the United Nations Charter established in 1945. Coming after two bitter, brutal world wars, the UN Charter codified the territorial integrity of all states, and identified the crime of aggression as the ultimate violation of international law.

But the European order that gradually emerged towards the end of the Cold War went further than this. Through the laborious negotiations leading up to the Helsinki Accords in 1975, and through the process that produced the Paris Charter of 1990, Europeans added provisions on democracy, human rights, and economic cooperation to the basic security architecture.

Of course, there were occasional disagreements about how to implement these agreements’ requirements, and in both Georgia and Moldova in the 2000s, Russia openly violated provisions barring the presence of a country’s armed forces on the territory of another without its consent.

These moves sparked bitter debates, with Russia eventually calling for revisions to the European security order. The Kremlin, for obvious reasons, objected to the provisions concerning human rights and elections, and demanded that they be deleted or substantially diluted.

It wasn’t difficult to see why. A series of “colour revolutions” had started to sweep through the region, most notably in Georgia and Ukraine, where protesters demanded democratic reforms, the rule of law, and closer links with democratic Europe.
Upon returning to the presidency after a brief stint as prime minister to circumvent constitutional limits, Putin himself was confronted with huge demonstrations in Moscow.

With a democratic wave sweeping much of the world at the time, the Kremlin understood that the colour revolutions in other countries had inspired pro-democracy demonstrations on its own streets. More to the point, it knew that pro-democratic forces could count on moral support from the West.

Russia tried to force new negotiations to suppress previously agreed commitments on democracy, but no one else would support such an effort. The order that had been established at the summits in Helsinki and Paris stood firm.

More recently, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov has called attention to a provision from a 1999 Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe document, which holds that signatories “will not strengthen their security at the expense of the security of other states”.

Yet he completely ignores another provision from the same document, which reaffirms “the inherent right of each and every participating state to be free to choose or change its security arrangements, including treaties of alliance”.
Such cynical cherry picking is dishonest even by Lavrov’s standards. Membership in Nato or the European Union clearly preserves peace and in no way threatens Russia.

Democratisation in other countries may well inspire those seeking democratic change inside Russia, but that is not the democratising countries’ fault or problem, nor does it endanger Russia’s security.
Putin is now left trying to roll back various European countries’ security choices, and thus their sovereignty. This is obviously a non-starter.

Finland and Sweden chose to enter Nato not to attack Russia, but because Russia had just launched a full-scale invasion of another European neighbour. No sane person is under any illusion about cause and effect.

One hopes that at some point there will be an opening to return to confidence-building and arms-control measures. But with Russian guns blazing and Russian bombs falling over another European country’s civilian centres, now is obviously not the time.

The European security order’s foundational principle is to reject aggression and respect other countries’ territorial integrity. There is no need to revise that order, only to wait for a Russian regime that is willing to accept it.
In the next round of talks, European representatives will demand an immediate end to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. Until that happens, there is nothing else to talk about.
Carl Bildt is a former prime minister and foreign minister of Sweden.
